Experiment: Step1: Define objectives and design-of-experiments (DOE): target 2.4 µm-thick epitaxial YBa2Cu3O7−δ films on LaMnO3/MgO/Y2O3/Al2O3/Hastelloy with embedded BaHfO3 (BHO) nanocrystals; primary responses are Jc(B,T) at 4.2–50 K up to 9 T, self-field Ic at 77 K (12 mm width), texture metrics, and microstructural descriptors (particle size/density, stacking fault and Y248 density, local strain); factors: pristine BHO size {3, 5.5, 10 nm}, BHO loading {5, 10, 15, 20 mol% relative to YBCO formula units}, pure YBCO seed layer thickness {200, 300 nm}, high-temperature growth dwell time {20, 40, 60 min}; include at least 2 replicates per condition and center points (5.5 nm, 10 mol%, 250 nm seed, 40 min dwell) for statistical robustness.

Step2: Prepare substrates: obtain industrial LaMnO3/MgO/Y2O3/Al2O3/Hastelloy tapes with confirmed biaxial texture (Δφ ≤ 7°, Δω ≤ 3°); clean reels by solvent wipe (acetone, isopropanol), mild O2 plasma (1–2 min) to remove organics; bake at 150 °C to remove moisture; store in dry N2.

Step3: Synthesize BHO nanocrystals (polyol solvothermal): prepare three batches targeting 3±0.5 nm, 5.5±0.5 nm, and 10±1 nm; dissolve barium and hafnium precursors in ethylene glycol with controlled water content and polymeric stabilizer (e.g., PVP) and base (e.g., NaOH) to tune nucleation/growth; typical reaction 180–220 °C for 30–120 min under N2 with vigorous stirring; quench; wash by repeated precipitation–redispersion in ethanol and acetone to remove excess organics.

Step4: Ligand management and solvent exchange for MOD compatibility: perform ligand exchange to weakly bound carboxylate (propionate or acetate) in propionic acid/ethanol to render BHO dispersible in MOD solution; employ brief low-temperature ozone or UV-ozone treatment on wet-cast BHO films to screen organics if necessary; verify minimal residual carbon by TGA/DSC and FTIR.

Step5: Characterize pristine BHO dispersions: transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and dynamic light scattering to confirm core size and hydrodynamic size; XRD to verify perovskite BHO; measure zeta potential in target MOD solvent to ensure colloidal stability (|ζ| ≥ 25 mV).

Step6: Prepare low-fluorine MOD YBCO precursor solution: use metal carboxylate salts (Y, Ba, Cu propionates or acetates) in propionic acid–alcohol solvent mixture; adjust stoichiometry to Y:Ba:Cu = 1:2:3 with low F/Ba ratio; set solids content and viscosity to yield ~200–300 nm per coat on tape at selected coating speed; filter through 0.2 µm PTFE filter.

Step7: Calibrate BHO addition: define “mol% BHO” as molar ratio of BaHfO3 to YBa2Cu3O7 formula units; compute required mass of BHO for each mol% using densities and molecular weights; prepare BHO-doped MOD solutions at 5, 10, 15, 20 mol% for each pristine size; stabilize by adding small amount of compatible dispersant (e.g., propionic acid) and ultrasonicate (bath 30 min + probe 2–5 min, cooling to avoid heating); verify no visible agglomeration and DLS monomodal distribution.

Step8: Establish coating line parameters (reel-to-reel): set line speed and drying conditions to achieve uniform wet thickness; use slot-die or dip-coating with nitrogen hood to control ambient humidity; use contactless IR heaters for staged drying before pyrolysis; collect coupons (10–15 cm length) at multiple positions to assess uniformity.

Step9: Deposit pure YBCO seed layer: coat with BHO-free MOD solution to target 200 or 300 nm after conversion; staged drying at 80–120 °C to remove solvent; pyrolysis under flowing O2 (or air) with controlled humidity: ramp 1–3 °C/min to 350 °C, hold 30 min; ramp to 425 °C, hold 30–60 min to remove organics and form precursor oxide; avoid rapid heating to prevent film cracking.

Step10: Crystallize seed layer: ramp 10 °C/min to 785 °C in low pO2 (e.g., 200–400 ppm O2 in N2) to promote epitaxial YBCO; hold 20–40 min; cool to 720 °C at 5–10 °C/min, then to 500 °C; switch to pure O2 at 500 °C and hold 30–60 min; cool to room temperature; record temperature and pO2 profiles.

Step11: Deposit BHO-doped YBCO layers (multistep to 2.1–2.2 µm): perform sequential coats of BHO-doped solution; for each coat, staged drying and pyrolysis identical to Step9; implement a “stacked conversion” strategy: after every 3–4 coats (≈0.6–0.8 µm cumulative), perform high-temperature epitaxial growth at 785 °C (low pO2) with dwell time per DOE setting (20, 40, or 60 min); include one intermediate cool to 500 °C O2 between growth cycles; repeat until total thickness reaches 2.4 µm including seed.

Step12: Oxygenation anneal: after final growth, cool to 500 °C, switch to pure O2, hold 1–5 h to oxygenate YBCO; slow cool to room temperature in O2; target δ ≈ 0.07–0.1; verify later by Tc.

Step13: Control experiments for coarsening kinetics: prepare small coupon sets from center-point condition; vary dwell times at 785 °C (10, 20, 40, 60, 90 min) keeping all else constant; use these to derive BHO coarsening curves and final size distributions; correlate with 3 nm vs 5.5 nm starting size.

Step14: Thickness and surface morphology: measure thickness by stylus profilometry on laser-etched step edge; confirm via cross-sectional SEM; assess surface roughness by AFM; aim for RMS < 20 nm.

Step15: Phase and texture assessment by XRD: collect θ–2θ scans to confirm c-axis oriented YBCO and presence of BHO reflections; perform rocking curves (ω scans) of YBCO (00l) peaks to quantify out-of-plane mosaic; φ scans of YBCO (103) and substrate reference peaks to quantify in-plane texture; ensure BHO addition does not broaden Δω or Δφ beyond acceptable limits.

Step16: Electrical resistivity and Tc: measure R(T) from 300 K to 20 K on 3–5 mm wide bridges; determine Tc onset and transition width; target Tc ≥ 90 K with narrow transition (<1 K) for well-oxygenated films; if Tc suppressed, adjust oxygenation anneal.

Step17: Cross-sectional FIB lamella preparation: select representative regions; deposit protective Pt cap; mill lamellae with low-kV final polish to minimize damage; prepare multiple lamellae across width to assess uniformity through thickness.

Step18: STEM-HAADF and EDX/EELS: image cross-sections to quantify BHO particle size distribution and spatial density in each condition; map Hf, Ba, Y, Cu, O to confirm BHO identity and exclude secondary Cu/Ba phases; assess BHO location uniformity and absence of agglomeration.

Step19: High-resolution TEM and defect analysis: identify Y248 intergrowths, stacking faults, and twin boundaries; quantify areal density of intergrowths and fault spacing; correlate with BHO presence and size.

Step20: Geometric phase analysis (GPA): perform strain mapping (εxx, εyy) around BHO nanocrystals and intergrowths from HRTEM images; quantify strain amplitude and decay length; compile statistics across dozens of particles per sample.

Step21: Particle statistics and spacing: compute volume fraction and number density of BHO from STEM images; derive mean interparticle spacing d ≈ n^(-1/3) and compare with particle diameters; calculate pin volume fraction; use these to estimate optimal matching to 2ξ(T) across measurement temperatures.

Step22: Depth profiling of Hf distribution: perform STEM-EDX line scans and, if available, GDOES on reference films to confirm uniform Hf through the doped thickness and sharp interface at the seed layer.

Step23: Mechanical integrity: bend tests on doped and undoped samples to radii corresponding to tensile strain 0.2–0.5%; remeasure 77 K self-field Ic to check strain tolerance; inspect for cracking by SEM.

Step24: Contact metallization for transport: deposit Ag (e.g., sputtered 200–500 nm) on top; solder or silver-epoxy current and voltage taps; for full-width 12 mm tests, use end contacts and side voltage taps separated by 5–10 cm; for patterned bridges, laser-scribe to 1–3 mm width as needed for magnet measurements.

Step25: 77 K self-field Ic measurements: use standard four-probe method with 1 µV/cm criterion; measure multiple segments along the tape length to assess uniformity; record n-values from V–I curves; target high Ic with minimal degradation versus undoped reference for each BHO condition.

Step26: Low-temperature, high-field Jc(B,T) by transport: measure at 4.2 K, 20 K, and 30 K in fields up to 9 T; align field orientations for θ = 0° (H||c) and 90° (H||ab); extract Jc from Ic by using measured cross-section (width × thickness); compute lifting factor Jc(B)/Jc(self-field) at 4.2 K and 30 K; identify Bp (field at maximum pinning force Fp).

Step27: Magnetization measurements (SQUID-VSM or VSM): cut small rectangular strips; measure M–H loops at 4.2–50 K for H||c and H||ab; use Bean model for rectangular slabs to extract Jc(H,T); compare with transport values as cross-check; ensure demagnetization factors are accounted for.

Step28: Angular dependence Ic(θ): at 77 K and 4.2 K, measure Ic vs θ in fixed fields (e.g., 1, 3, 5, 9 T); look for isotropic enhancement expected from spherical BHO; quantify anisotropy ratio Jc(90°)/Jc(0°).

Step29: Pinning force scaling: compute Fp = μ0 Jc B; plot reduced pinning force fp vs reduced field b = B/Bc2(T) (or use empirical scaling with Bp); fit Dew-Hughes exponents to distinguish point-like core pinning dominance; examine shifts in Bp with BHO size and density.

Step30: Upper critical field estimation and ξ(T): measure resistive Hc2(T) near Tc for H||c and H||ab via transport under field; estimate coherence length ξab(T) from Hc2; compare particle diameter and mean spacing to 2ξ(T) to rationalize optimal conditions.

Step31: Connectivity and grain boundary assessment: use scanning Hall probe microscopy or magneto-optical imaging to visualize current percolation; compare undoped and BHO-doped samples for weak-link behavior; analyze linearity of Ic reduction with increased BHO loading.

Step32: Texture preservation verification: correlate XRD rocking curve widths and φ-scans with Ic and Jc; ensure BHO addition does not broaden texture beyond thresholds that would limit percolative paths; if degradation observed, adjust seed thickness or reduce BHO loading.

Step33: Process optimization loop: based on microstructure–property correlations, select optimal pristine BHO size (anticipated around 5.5 nm), loading (around 10 mol%), and dwell time (favoring minimal coarsening while achieving epitaxy); fine-tune dwell and oxygenation to balance particle growth and strain-field preservation.

Step34: Long-length uniformity tests: coat and process ≥10 m length under optimal parameters; sample every 0.5–1 m for 77 K self-field Ic and at least three positions for 4.2 K, 1–3 T Jc; compile statistics (mean, σ/mean) to assess manufacturability.

Step35: Thermal budget sensitivity: vary growth temperature ±10–15 °C around 785 °C for optimal condition to probe robustness; reassess BHO size and Jc; define acceptable process window.

Step36: Chemical stability checks: XRD and TEM to ensure no reaction between BHO and YBCO (absence of BaCuO2, Y2BaCuO5); monitor Hf valence via EELS; if reactions detected, adjust pO2 during growth to stabilize chemical potentials.

Step37: Risk mitigation and troubleshooting: if BHO agglomeration observed, refine dispersion via higher-energy ultrasonication, solvent polarity adjustment, or lower solids content per coat; if carbonate residues form during pyrolysis, increase humidity control and adjust heating rates; if texture degrades, increase seed thickness or reduce per-cycle thickness before crystallization.

Step38: Benchmarking against requirements: confirm at optimal parameters that Jc at 4.2–30 K maintains high values up to 9 T while 77 K self-field Ic remains above target thresholds; ensure angular Jc shows reduced anisotropy indicative of isotropic pinning; document lifting factors at relevant fields and temperatures.

Step39: Application-relevant tests: perform short-coil or racetrack sample winding with optimal conductor; measure Ic before and after winding at 77 K and 4.2 K; evaluate degradation under operational bend strains; if available, assess AC loss at 50–77 K for power applications.

Step40: Documentation and data integrity: record all solution compositions, coating parameters, temperature/pO2 profiles, and characterization data; maintain traceability between microstructure and performance for each DOE condition; prepare protocols for scale-up under reel-to-reel production constraints.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1 – BHO nanocrystal synthesis  
- Reagents: hafnium (IV) n-butoxide (60 % in n-butanol, 22.6 wt % Hf) and barium hydroxide.  
- Solvent: triethylene glycol + ethanol (EtOH).  
- Process: microwave solvothermal treatment at 180 °C, 300 W, 2.45 GHz, 60 min in a TANK eco-microwave reactor.  
- Output: mono-dispersed BHO nanocrystals (500 mM in EtOH, surface-capped with 2-[2-(2-methoxyethoxy)ethoxy]).

Step 2 – YBCO precursor preparation  
- Low-fluorine MOD route (reference [21] cited; exact fluorine content not given).  
- BHO nanocrystals added directly to the precursor at 0–20 mol % relative to Y content; four discrete sizes prepared.

Step 3 – Coating architecture  
- Substrate: industrial 5-layer tape LaMnO₃/MgO/Y₂O₃/Al₂O₃/Hastelloy.  
- Seed layer: 200–300 nm pure YBCO precursor first coated to act as self-seeding layer.  
- Main layer: three successive coats of BHO-doped YBCO precursor; total YBCO thickness 2.4 µm.  
- Each coat pyrolysed ≈ 20 min (temperature not specified).

Step 4 – Crystallisation heat treatment  
Reconstructed from multiple sections of the PDF:  
- Multistep growth: one-third of conventional growth at 785 °C → direct cooling → re-heating through full conventional profile; total high-temperature dwell ≈ 40 min.  
- Atmosphere, heating/cooling rates, and oxygenation details not explicitly described.

Step 5 – Microstructural characterisation  
- TEM: JEOL JEM-2100 F field-emission HRTEM for BHO size distributions; cross-sections prepared by FEI Helios Nanolab 600i FIB.  
- STEM: high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) imaging and geometric phase analysis (GPA) for local strain mapping.  
- XRD: powder patterns of as-synthesised BHO (instrument not specified).

Step 6 – Superconducting property measurements  
- Magnetisation: Quantum Design Physical Property Measurement System; hysteresis loops taken at 4.2 K, 30 K, 50 K, 77 K in fields up to 9 T.  
- Jc calculation: extended Bean model (reference [22]).  
- Transport Ic: 1-m-long tapes tested with EASTFORCE M-Corder at 77 K, self-field; selected samples also measured at 30 K and under applied field (angle-dependent data collected).  
- Pinning force density Fp derived from magnetisation Jc(B).

Step 7 – Data analysis  
- Size statistics from TEM images (>100 particles).  
- Coarsening factor = final BHO size / pristine BHO size.  
- Particle density estimated assuming random uniform distribution.  
- Performance metrics: Jc(B,T), Ic(77 K, self-field), normalised enhancement η = Jc/Jc,pure, lift factor Jc(4.2 K)/Jc(77 K, 0 T).

[Experimental Design Details]
- Sample matrix: 4 pristine BHO sizes × 4 concentrations (5, 10, 15, 20 mol %) → 16 BHO–YBCO variants plus pure YBCO reference.  
- Final BHO sizes after heat treatment:  
  – 3.0 nm → 20 ± 13 nm (coarsening factor 6.3)  
  – 5.5 nm → 7.0 ± 3 nm (1.28)  
  – 8.0 nm → 9.3 ± 4 nm (1.17)  
  – 10.0 nm → 10.9 ± 4 nm (1.09)  
- Highest particle density: 20.5 × 10²¹ m⁻³ for 5.5 nm, 10 mol % case.  
- Best in-field Jc at 4.2 K, 1 T: 20.8 MA cm⁻² (5.5 nm, 10 mol %).  
- Transport Ic (77 K, self-field, 12 mm width): up to 827 A for 8.0 nm, 5 mol %; 5.5 nm samples give highest Ic at low temperature and moderate field.

pred_experiment:
Experiment: Step1: Substrate and texture verification: Receive 4 mm-wide Hastelloy C-276 tapes buffered with IBAD-MgO/LaMnO3 (LMO). Verify biaxial texture by XRD: measure MgO and LMO φ-scans and rocking curves; accept Δφ ≤5° and Δω ≤3°. Reject or re-clean tapes not meeting texture criteria.

Step2: PLD target preparation and qualification: Fabricate dense, crack-free 2-inch (or 3-inch) ceramic targets:
- EuBa2Cu3O7−δ + BaHfO3 at 2, 3.5, and 5 mol% BHO (molar % relative to REBCO), pressed and sintered ≥940 °C in flowing O2; polish surface to 1 μm finish.
- YBa2Cu3O7−δ with Y-excess of 5, 15, and 25 mol% (to induce Y2O3 nanoprecipitation), sintered ≥930 °C in O2; polish surface.
Confirm phase purity by powder XRD (REBCO dominant, perovskite-like BHO reflections for Eu targets; no secondary cuprates >5%) and density ≥95% theoretical. Measure target ablation rates on witness substrates to ensure stable plume.

Step3: PLD tool setup and calibration: Configure the LEAP-300C (300 Hz) PLD system with multi-target carousel and load-lock. Set target–substrate distance 6–7 cm; laser fluence 1.2–1.6 J/cm²; spot homogenized to avoid local overheating. Install a heated rotating drum or flat heater stage with tape transport. Calibrate substrate temperature with a thermocouple or optical pyrometer against a standard; establish 770–800 °C at the film surface. Verify oxygen/ozone delivery (O2 200–400 mTorr; optional 1–3% O3 admixture for improved epitaxy). Record base pressure (<1×10−6 Torr).

Step4: Deposition rate calibration on witnesses: Using MgO(100) or LMO/MgO single-crystal witnesses co-loaded with tape, deposit:
- EuBCO(BHO) at 300 Hz, 770–790 °C, pO2 200–250 mTorr; measure thickness by X-ray reflectivity (XRR) or profilometry to get nm/pulse; target 0.01–0.03 nm/pulse.
- YBCO(Y-excess) at 300 Hz, 770–790 °C, pO2 250–350 mTorr; obtain nm/pulse similarly.
Adjust laser fluence and tape speed to achieve desired growth rates (~1–2 μm total within practical run time).

Step5: Establish BHO nanorod inclination: Implement off-axis PLD geometry by tilting the substrate normal 10–20° relative to the plume axis (maintain in-plane azimuth fixed to tape transport direction). Use lower pO2 (≈200 mTorr) and moderate growth rate (≥0.01 nm/pulse) to promote self-assembled, c-axis–correlated BHO nanorods with a controlled inclination relative to the film c-axis. Validate inclination on a 200–300 nm pilot EuBCO(BHO) film by cross-sectional STEM (see Step13) before full-length runs.

Step6: EuBCO(BHO-NR) layer deposition (bottom layer): Mount tape (length for R&D: 1–5 m) on the heated stage. Heat to 780 ± 10 °C in 200–250 mTorr O2. Pre-ablate the EuBCO(BHO) target for 2–5 min to stabilize the plume. Deposit EuBCO(BHO) with the established tilt geometry:
- Select BHO content (start with 3.5 mol%).
- Control thickness between 0.8 and 1.6 μm (≤1.65 μm) by tape speed and pulses (from Step4); maintain uniform rotation/translation.
- Use brief dwell/pause segments (e.g., 2–5 s pauses every 50–100 μm equivalent thickness) if pilot STEM indicates continuous rods that exceed ~40 nm; this encourages segmentation of rods.
After growth, maintain temperature for 2–3 min in deposition pO2 to relax strain, then ramp to the YBCO deposition condition without breaking vacuum.

Step7: YBCO(YO-NP) layer deposition (top layer): Switch to the Y-excess YBCO target without inserting a spacer. Raise pO2 to 300–350 mTorr while keeping substrate at 770–790 °C. Deposit:
- Begin with 15 mol% Y-excess; thickness 0.8–1.6 μm (≤1.65 μm) such that total bilayer thickness ≤3.1 μm.
- Maintain normal-incidence geometry (no tilt) to avoid directional pins and favor random YO nanoparticle precipitation.
- Avoid long high-temperature dwell between layers to limit interdiffusion; complete target swap and deposition restart within ≤30 s.
Cool to 500–550 °C in 300–500 mTorr O2 at 5–10 °C/min.

Step8: Ex-situ oxygenation: Transfer tapes to a tube furnace. Anneal in flowing O2 (1 bar) at 350–380 °C for 8–12 h; cool to room temperature at 1–3 °C/min. This optimizes carrier concentration (δ ≈ 0.07–0.1) and relieves interfacial stress.

Step9: Ag cap deposition: DC sputter a 2 μm Ag cap at ≤120 °C substrate temperature to avoid deoxygenation. Optionally include a 50–100 nm Au wetting layer for improved contact resistance on microbridges.

Step10: Control samples for deconvolution: In parallel, fabricate single-layer controls on identical tape sections:
- EuBCO(BHO) only (thickness matched to bilayer Eu layer).
- YBCO(Y-excess) only (thickness matched to bilayer Y layer).
Use identical process conditions to enable linear superposition analysis.

Step11: Texture and phase confirmation: Perform XRD θ–2θ scans to confirm c-axis orientation of both layers (00ℓ peaks only), and φ-scans/rocking curves on the bilayer to ensure Δφ ≤5°. Check for parasitic phases (e.g., BaCuO2, CuO) below detection or minimized.

Step12: Electrical oxygenation check: Measure Tc by four-probe resistivity on 1–2 mm sections or by magnetization; accept Tc onset ≥92 K and transition width ≤1.5 K. If Tc is low or broad, repeat oxygen anneal (e.g., 375 °C, 6 h).

Step13: Microstructure analysis (STEM/EDS): Prepare cross-sectional lamellae by FIB at representative positions (bottom Eu layer, interface, top Y layer). Acquire HAADF-STEM and EDS maps:
- Eu layer: verify BHO nanorods aligned approximately along c with intended inclination; measure rod length (~40 nm), diameter (typically 3–8 nm), areal density, and tilt angle distribution. If rods are continuous through thickness, adjust Step6 (growth rate/pauses) and Step5 (tilt, pO2) in the next iteration.
- Y layer: quantify YO nanoparticle size distribution (target 10–30 nm tablet-like), spacing, and random orientation. Confirm absence of secondary rod-like APCs.
- Interface: confirm epitaxial registry and absence of amorphous interlayers; quantify interdiffusion width by EDS/EELS (<3–5 nm).

Step14: Surface morphology: AFM on decapped or Ag-thinned areas to measure RMS roughness (target ≤5 nm over 5×5 μm²) to ensure good current percolation and cap adhesion.

Step15: Microbridge patterning for transport: Define 50 μm-wide bridges (length 0.5–1.0 mm) by photolithography + Ar ion milling or by UV laser scribing through Ag + REBCO. Deposit/define contact pads (Au/Ag). Confirm bridge geometry by optical microscopy and profilometry.

Step16: Four-probe transport setup: Mount patterned samples on a low-thermal-mass rotator. Wire contacts with silver paste or indium solder; cure appropriately. Connect to a cryogen-free 15 T magnet with a rotator and a Hall-based angle encoder. Calibrate angle zero with respect to tape normal; define θ = 0° for B∥c and θ = 90° for B∥ab. Install a Cernox sensor adjacent to the bridge; verify temperature stability ±0.1 K.

Step17: Jc(B,T,θ) measurements: At T = 65, 71, 77, and 81 K, measure E–I curves at B = 0.1–15 T for θ from 0° to 180° in 2° (fine ±0.5° near 0° and 90°). Use a 1 μV/cm criterion for Jc; limit power dissipation (pulsed current or short dwell) to avoid self-heating. Record n-values (slope of E∝I^n) for AC loss relevance.

Step18: Anisotropy factor computation: For each (T,B), compute:
- Jc,max = maxθ∈[0°,90°] Jc(θ); Jc,min = minθ∈[0°,90°] Jc(θ).
- Anisotropy factor A = 1 − (Jc,min/Jc,max). Target A ≤ 0.55 for 65–77 K at B ≤3 T.
Also explicitly record Jc(θ≈0°) and Jc(θ≈90°) to monitor peaks from correlated (BHO) and point-like (YO) pins.

Step19: Acceptance criteria and go/no-go: Acceptance if:
- Jc ≥ 1×10^4 A/cm² at 77 K, 3 T, B∥c.
- A ≤ 0.55 at 65–77 K for B ≤3 T.
- n-value ≥ 20 at 77 K, 3 T (for stable operation).
If unmet, branch to Step22 for parameter adjustment.

Step20: Superposition validation with controls: Measure Jc(B,T,θ) on single-layer EuBCO(BHO) and YBCO(Y-excess) controls (Step10). Convert to layer currents I_layer = Jc_layer × t_layer × w_bridge. Fit bilayer current I_total(θ) at target (T,B) to I_fit(θ) = α I_Y(θ) + β I_Eu(θ). Evaluate α,β near unity; assess goodness-of-fit (R² ≥ 0.95). Significant deviations trigger interface or connectivity diagnostics (Step13, Step21).

Step21: Pinning analysis: Apply anisotropic Ginzburg–Landau scaling to separate isotropic and correlated pin contributions. Extract pinning force Fp(B) and Kramer plots to estimate Hirr at 77 K (target ≈9 T). Correlate rod density/tilt (Step13) and YO NP size (Step13) with peaks in Jc(θ). Use this to guide subsequent tuning.

Step22: Design-of-experiments (DOE) optimization: Iterate across the following matrix:
- BHO content: 2, 3.5, 5 mol% (Eu layer).
- Y-excess: 5, 15, 25 mol% (Y layer).
- Thickness ratio t_Y:t_Eu: 0.6, 1.0, 1.4 (with each layer ≤1.65 μm, total ≤3.1 μm).
- Nanorod tilt: 10°, 15°, 20° (via substrate tilt and pO2).
For each variant, repeat Steps6–20 on short (1–2 m) sections; select the recipe minimizing A while meeting Jc thresholds at 65–77 K, ≤3 T.

Step23: Mechanical/electromechanical robustness: Measure Ic vs axial strain using a Walters spring at 77 K, 3 T and at 65 K, 3 T. Apply strain from −0.2% to +0.4% in 0.05% steps; record reversible range and irreversible strain (εirr). Target no cracking or >5% Ic loss up to ≥0.3% tensile strain. If degradation occurs, reduce total thickness or adjust post-anneal (Step8) to mitigate tensile residual strain.

Step24: Long-length uniformity pilot: Implement the optimized recipe on a 50–100 m tape using a multi-turn pass (first Eu layer, switch targets, then Y layer in the same vacuum cycle if possible). Sample every 10 m: cut microbridges or use non-destructive Hall-probe scanning and local transport at 77 K, 3 T to verify Jc uniformity (≤±10%). Perform XRD texture check on start, middle, end sections.

Step25: Process controls and monitoring: During deposition, log tape speed, heater temperature, pO2, laser energy (±2%), target wear, and carousel timing. Use in-situ plume imaging or optical emission to monitor stability. Implement target resurfacing every ~30–60 minutes at 300 Hz to maintain constant ablation.

Step26: Risk mitigation and troubleshooting:
- If interface shows intermixing >5 nm or degraded superposition fit, reduce interlayer dwell time and deposition temperature by 10–20 °C for the first 100–200 nm of the Y layer, then ramp back.
- If BHO rods are too vertical or too long, increase tilt angle to 15–20°, slightly lower pO2, and introduce deposition pauses (Step6).
- If YO particles exceed 30 nm or cluster, reduce Y-excess and/or slightly increase pO2 to 350–400 mTorr to limit coarsening.
- If texture degrades, verify substrate cleanliness and reduce growth rate.

Step27: Documentation and data management: Record all deposition parameters, microstructure metrics (rod tilt, length, density; YO NP size distribution), and Jc(B,T,θ) datasets. Archive raw STEM/EDS and XRD data. Maintain traceability between tape ID, recipe, and performance.

Step28: Reporting and down-select: Summarize the best-performing bilayer recipe with:
- Eu layer: BHO mol%, thickness, rod tilt/length metrics.
- Y layer: Y-excess, thickness, YO NP size distribution.
- Performance: Jc(77 K, 3 T, B∥c), A(65–77 K, ≤3 T), Hirr(77 K), n-values, strain tolerance.
Confirm readiness for scale-up to motor/generator coil-lengths based on uniformity and robustness.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1 – Substrate preparation  
Start from commercial buffered metallic tapes: Hastelloy C-276 / Al₂O₃ / Y₂O₃ / IBAD-MgO / LaMnO₃. (No further substrate fabrication details are given.)

Step 2 – Target preparation (not experimentally detailed)  
Prepare two separate ceramic targets:  
- EuBCO + 2–5 mol % BaHfO₃ (for nano-rods)  
- YBCO + 5–25 mol % excess Y (for Y₂O₃ nano-particles)  
Exact dopant concentrations are proprietary and not disclosed.

Step 3 – Pulsed-laser deposition (PLD) of REBCO layers  
Deposit REBCO layers at Faraday Factory Japan LLC using a Coherent LEAP-300C laser (300 Hz, 900–1000 mJ pulse energy).  
- Eu-NR sample: single EuBCO layer, tEu-NR = 1.58 µm.  
- Y-NP sample: single YBCO layer, tY-NP = 1.85 µm.  
- Eu-NR/Y-NP bilayer: first deposit 1.65 µm EuBCO (Eu-NR), then deposit 1.45 µm YBCO (Y-NP) without breaking vacuum, giving total REBCO thickness 3.1 µm.  
Substrate temperature, oxygen pressure, and growth rate are not specified.

Step 4 – Ag protection layer  
Immediately after REBCO growth, cover the film with 2 µm Ag by magnetron sputtering at room temperature.

Step 5 – Oxygenation anneal  
Anneal the finished tapes at 300–400 °C for 12 h in flowing O₂ to optimize carrier concentration. Heating/cooling profiles are not provided.

Step 6 – Micro-bridge patterning

Step2: Configure the PLD-VLS system. Use a KrF excimer laser (248 nm) with a stoichiometric YBa2Cu3O7−δ ceramic target (density > 95%). Use a heated substrate stage with calibrated pyrometry/thermocouple at 860–940 °C and a controlled O2 partial pressure (53–200 Pa). Implement substrate rotation and target rastering. Ensure base pressure < 1×10⁻⁵ Pa before backfilling O2. Install an in-situ optical reflectometer (or video microscope) to monitor surface morphology and a residual gas analyzer to track O2/H2O.

Step3: Map the VLS growth window. Deposit short (100–200 nm) YBCO trials at T = 880, 900, 920, 940 °C and pO2 = 60, 100, 150, 200 Pa, keeping other parameters fixed. After each trial: ex-situ XRD 2θ–ω to confirm c-axis orientation; SEM to assess smoothness and presence of nanoscale droplets; four-probe Tc after oxygenation (see Step7). Identify conditions giving (i) dominant (00l) peaks with negligible (200)/(020), (ii) smooth surfaces with occasional sub-micron Cu-rich droplets (by EDX), and (iii) Tc ≥ 90 K. Target a process window around 890–920 °C and 80–150 Pa where Ba–Cu–O liquid exists at the growth front (VLS regime) without decomposing the buffer.

Step4: Optional VLS wetting layer validation. For a subset, pre-deposit a 2–5 nm Ba–Cu–O wetting layer by ablating a BaCuO2–CuO mixed target or by 5–10 laser pulses at elevated T before YBCO growth. Compare with samples without prelayer to see whether VLS regime is more robust (smoother surfaces, fewer a-axis grains). Keep overall Y:Ba:Cu stoichiometry near 1:2:3 by adjusting subsequent YBCO deposition time.

Step5: Establish thickness calibration. For the chosen VLS window, grow YBCO films with nominal thickness 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 µm using time-based control. Determine the actual growth rate by cross-sectional SEM on cleaved edges and profilometer step heights made by masking part of the substrate. Iterate laser repetition rate to achieve a stable growth rate (±5%) across a 50 mm length.

Step6: Deposit the thickness series under identical VLS conditions. Prepare at least 3 replicates at each target thickness: 0.94, 1.5, 2.3, 3.0, and 3.7 µm. Use the same substrate architecture batch, same T and pO2, same laser fluence and repetition rate. To sustain VLS: (i) maintain constant pO2 within ±5 Pa, (ii) incorporate 1–2 min dwell every ~0.5–0.7 µm at growth temperature without plume to allow surface liquid redistribution/healing, and (iii) avoid plume oversupply (keep supersaturation low by not exceeding 10 Hz). Monitor surface reflectance; if reflectance oscillations damp or surface appears rough, pause deposition for 2–3 min to re-establish a smooth front.

Step7: Post-deposition oxygenation. After growth, cool in O2 from Tgrowth to 500 °C at 10–15 °C min⁻¹, hold 0.5 h at 500 °C (pO2 ≥ 10 kPa), then ramp to 450 °C and anneal 12–24 h in flowing O2 (1 bar). Cool slowly to 350 °C (1–2 °C min⁻¹) and then to room temperature to achieve y ≈ 6.9–6.95. This minimizes residual stress and maximizes Tc. For very thick films (≥ 3 µm), extend the 450 °C anneal to 24 h.

Step8: Verify composition and thickness. Measure thickness by cross-section SEM for each sample (at 3–5 positions along length) and by stylus profilometry at a masked step. Determine Y:Ba:Cu ratios by ICP-OES on a small sacrificial piece; target 1:2:3 within ±2%. Cross-check with EDX area scans. Reject samples with >3% deviation.

Step9: Quantify phase purity and texture. Perform XRD 2θ–ω scans to confirm c-axis oriented YBCO (00l) reflections only; quantify the a-axis fraction by integrating (200)/(020) peak intensities corrected for geometry, reporting a-axis grain ratio with a detection limit ~0.1–0.3%. Step10: Map surface morphology and precipitates. Use SEM (5–10 kV) and AFM (5×5 µm² scans) to measure RMS roughness and identify secondary phase precipitates. Use SEM-EDX point analysis and maps to confirm precipitates are Cu-rich (Ba–Cu–O) and to ensure their aerial density and size (typically tens–hundreds of nm) do not increase dramatically with thickness. Step16: Magnetic relaxation to derive U*. At fixed T (30, 50, 60, 70, 77 K) and H (e.g., 1, 2, 3 T) with H ∥ c, record M(t) for 10³–10⁴ s starting from a well-defined initial state (field ramp to target, wait 60 s, start acquisition). Compute the normalized creep rate S = d ln|M|/d ln t. Convert M to J using the Bean model, then compute the apparent activation energy U*(J,T,H) = kB T/S. Plot U*(J) and U*(H) for each thickness.

Step17: E–J from magnetization relaxation. Using the relation E ≈ −(dB/dt)·(effective length scale) inferred from dM/dt in thin films, reconstruct E(J) curves at 60–77 K and compare with transport E–J to extract the n-value (E ∝ Jⁿ) and confirm the creep regime. Ensure consistent n within ±10–20% between magnetization-derived and transport measurements.

Step18: Collective creep analysis and correlation length. Fit U(J) to the collective creep form U(J) = Uc (Jc/J)^μ. Extract μ and Uc for each thickness and temperature. If a thickness-dependent increase in Uc is observed, correlate with reductions in S and increases in transport n-values.

Step19: Pinning force scaling. Compute Fp = Jc·B from transport and magnetization data. Prepare 1–2 µm and 3 µm controls. Characterize texture (Δω, Δϕ), a-axis fraction, roughness, and measure Jc and U*. Compare to VLS-grown films to isolate the role of VLS in maintaining texture and improving creep behavior at larger thickness.

Step21: Droplet density tuning. Within the VLS window, vary pO2 modestly (±20–30 Pa) and laser repetition rate (±2 Hz) to modulate Ba–Cu–O droplet density without changing overall stoichiometry. Quantify droplet areal density and correlate with changes in Jc(H,77 K) and U*(H,77 K) to ensure that droplets act as benign pinning centers rather than degrading texture or Tc.

Step22: Stress and mechanical integrity tests. Perform wafer curvature measurements (if on coupon pieces) or XRD peak shift analysis to estimate residual strain versus thickness. Conduct repeated bend tests on tape segments (e.g., 5 mm radius, 100 cycles) and remeasure Jc(77 K, self-field and 2 T). Inspect by SEM for cracks or delamination. Document variation; aim for <20% Jc spread at 77 K, 2 T. If variability is high, examine plume homogeneity and substrate temperature uniformity.

Step24: Error analysis and statistics. Quantify uncertainties in thickness (±3–5%), bridge dimensions (±2%), voltage resolution, and geometry factors for Bean-model Jc. Propagate to Jc and U*. Report mean ± standard deviation across replicates for each thickness. Ensure consistent oxygenation by monitoring Tc and resistivity; exclude outliers with Tc < 90 K or anomalous R(T).

Step25: Decision criteria and outcome assessment. Consider the strategy successful if simultaneously: (i) Δω ≤ 0.72°, Δϕ ≤ 1.49°, a-axis fraction < 2.8% across all thicknesses; (ii) Tc ≥ 90 K; (iii) Jc(77 K, 2.0–2.5 T) increases monotonically with thickness, with the thickest (≈3.7 µm) exhibiting ≥ several-fold improvement over ~1 µm; (iv) U*(77 K, 2 T) increases with thickness and creep rates S decrease accordingly; and (v) no significant cracking/delamination is observed. Clean substrates with solvent rinse (acetone/isopropanol), UV-ozone or mild plasma to remove organics.

Step5: Design of experiments—composition series: deposit films with Zr mol% (relative to Ba) x = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 at fixed deposition temperature 775 °C, oxygen partial pressure 0.7 Torr, and rate 90 nm min−1 to a thickness of 0.55 µm. Use identical substrate texture class for all samples.

Step30: Data integration and selection for application: identify compositions and process windows that maximize Jc_min at 4–20 K across 0–30 T while maintaining robust texture; summarize structure–property links: Zr content → BZO rod density/length → Bφ and c-axis peak → Jc(B,θ); Ba compensation → interface sharpness and matrix integrity → high-field performance; oxygenation → Tc vs added point pinning from oxygen defects. Preserve samples for future coil-winding or electromechanical tests as next steps.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1: Substrate preparation – Use 12 mm-wide, 65 µm-thick Hastelloy substrates pre-coated with a 5-layer buffer stack: Al2O3/Y2O3/IBAD-MgO/homo-epitaxial MgO/LaMnO3.  
Step 2: Precursor solution preparation – Dissolve metal tetramethyl-heptanedionate (thd) compounds for Zr, Gd, Yb, Ba, and Cu in tetrahydrofuran (THF) at a fixed target cation ratio Gd:Yb:(Ba–Zr):Cu = 0.65:0.65:2.00:3.20. Prepare separate solutions for 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 mol% Zr addition levels.  
Step 3: Film deposition – Deposit 0.55 µm-thick Gd0.5Yb0.5BCO films via liquid-delivery MOCVD under fixed conditions: 775 °C substrate temperature, 2.0 Torr total chamber pressure, 0.7 Torr oxygen partial pressure, ~90 nm min−1 deposition rate.  
Step 4: Thickness verification – Measure final film thickness (0.51–0.62 µm) by cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy (TEM).  
Step 5: Composition verification – Determine actual Zr content and overall metal stoichiometry by electron probe microanalysis (EPMA).  
Step 6: Phase & texture characterization – Record 2D x-ray diffraction (2D-XRD) patterns at χ = 0° and 45° (Rigaku Smartlab 9000 W, HyPix-3000 detector) to identify REBCO, BaZrO3, BaCuO2 and RE2O3 phases and assess biaxial texture.  
Step 7: Microstructure imaging – Acquire cross-sectional and plan-view TEM images (JEOL JEM-2100 F) to visualize nanorod morphology, measure nanorod dimensions/spacing, and statistically evaluate number density (>600 nanorods counted per sample).  
Step 8: Critical temperature (Tc) measurement – Perform four-probe Tc measurement in a Quantum Design DynaCool-9 PPMS (details of temperature sweep rate or criterion not specified).  
Step 9: Transport critical current density (Jc) measurement – Pattern 1 mm × 5 mm bridges by laser lithography on 52 mm-long tape pieces; measure transport Jc at 4–77 K, 0–5 T using a standard four-probe method with 1 µV cm−1 criterion.  
Step 10: Magnetization Jc derivation at 4 K – Cut 2 × 2 mm² samples; measure M–B hysteresis loops in PPMS at 200 Oe s⁻¹ sweep rate; calculate Jc via Bean model (equation provided) and calibrate against transport Jc at (4 K, 5 T).  
Step 11: Angular Jc characterization – Rotate sample in magnetic field (1 T, 3 T, 5 T) at 20 K and 30 K; record Jc(θ) to evaluate pinning anisotropy.  
Step 12: High-field Jc extrapolation – Use power-law fit Jc(B)=Jc(0)·B^(−α) (α extracted from 4 K data) to extrapolate Jc beyond 14 T up to ~30 T.

[Experimental Design Details]
- Independent variable: nominal Zr addition level in precursor (0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 mol%).  
- Dependent variables: phase content, nanorod density/size, Tc, self-field Jc at 77 K & 4 K, in-field Jc(B,θ) at 4–77 K, power-law exponent α, crossover field Bcross.  
- Fixed processing parameters: substrate temperature 775 °C, total pressure 2.0 Torr, pO₂ 0.7 Torr, deposition rate ~90 nm min⁻¹, final film thickness ~0.55 µm, constant overall cation ratio.  
- Calibration: magnetic Jc(4 K) scaled to transport Jc(4 K, 5 T) to ensure consistency.  
- Statistics: nanorod density/width obtained by counting >600 rods across multiple plan-view TEM images for 15 and 25 mol% samples.

Experiment: Step1: Define objectives and variables. Goal: synthesize a carbonate-free BaCeO3/CeO2 nanocomposite (target crystallite sizes ≤35 nm) via reverse co-precipitation for incorporation into REBCO coated conductors as artificial pinning centers, and quantify the impact on Jc(B,T,θ) at intermediate temperatures and magnetic fields. Key variables: (i) Ce/Ba molar ratio in precursor (r = 1.0, 1.2, 1.5) to tune BaCeO3:CeO2 fraction; (ii) calcination temperature (800, 900, 1000 °C) and dwell (60 min) with rapid cooling (10 °C/min) vs slow cooling (2 °C/min); (iii) nanoparticle loading in REBCO precursor (1, 3, 5, 8 vol%); (iv) RE element (initially RE = Gd, with optional Y for controls); (v) substrate-buffer stack IBAD-MgO-based; (vi) processing atmosphere for REBCO conversion (pO2 ~100–300 ppm).

Step2: Laboratory preparation and safety. Use CO2-minimized environment for precipitation and washing: pre-boil and N2-degas DI water, cool under N2; perform precipitation in a N2-purged fume hood with CO2-scrubbed gas (soda-lime trap). Clean glassware by calcination (450 °C, 2 h) or acid wash and dry; store reagents in sealed containers. PPE: face shield, nitrile gloves, lab coat; handle Ba salts (toxic) and H2O2 (oxidizer) with care; neutralize ammoniacal effluents; capture NOx in DTA/TG-MS exhaust.

Step3: Prepare precursor solutions. Dissolve Ba(NO3)2 in CO2-free DI water to 0.1 M. Dissolve Ce(NO3)3·6H2O to 0.1 M. Prepare NH4OH (28–30 wt%) as base and H2O2 (30 wt%) as oxidant. Combine Ba and Ce nitrate solutions to achieve target Ce/Ba ratios r = 1.0, 1.2, 1.5. Keep total metal concentration ~0.05–0.1 M to limit local supersaturation spikes.

Step4: Reverse co-precipitation under CO2-free conditions. Under vigorous stirring at 25–30 °C in a N2 blanket, add NH4OH dropwise to the mixed Ba/Ce nitrate solution to raise pH gradually to 10.0–10.5 (monitor with a CO2-insensitive pH probe). Immediately during basification, feed H2O2 slowly (molar H2O2/Ce ≈ 2–3) to oxidize Ce3+→Ce4+ and promote CeO2 nucleation while forming Ba(OH)2·xH2O. Maintain stirring for 60 min; keep temperature ≤35 °C to limit Ostwald ripening. Age the suspension quiescently for 2 h to allow primary particle growth to the 5–15 nm scale.

Step5: Separation, washing, and drying. Separate precipitate by centrifugation (10,000 g, 10 min) or vacuum filtration using polypropylene membranes. Wash 3× with N2-degassed DI water to remove nitrates and ammonium; perform 2× final washes with ethanol or isopropanol to displace water. Dry the wet cake in a vacuum oven at 60–80 °C for 12 h. Store powder in N2-purged desiccators.

Step6: Thermal profiling by DTA/TG-MS. Analyze as-made powder (10–20 mg) in alumina pans, heating 30→1000 °C at 10 K min⁻¹ in dry air. Record mass loss and evolved gases (H2O, NOx, NH3, O2, CO2). Use this to set calcination profiles ensuring minimal carbonate uptake and complete decomposition of hydroxide/nitrate species. Expect main events: dehydration <200 °C; nitrate decomposition 200–500 °C; crystallization >600 °C. Confirm minimal CO2 evolution beyond background; if CO2 signal emerges, tighten CO2 controls in Steps 2–5.

Step7: Calcination and polymorph/size control. Place dried powder in pre-baked alumina crucibles; calcine in flowing dry air with 5 °C/min ramps to target temperatures (800, 900, 1000 °C), 60 min dwell; cool at either 10 °C/min (rapid-quench condition for stress tuning) or 2 °C/min (control). Prepare batches for each Ce/Ba ratio and temperature. Optionally, include a 600 °C/2 h intermediate hold to remove residual hydroxyls.

Step8: Phase and size quantification (powder). Perform XRD (Co Kα) scans 10–100° 2θ with high counting statistics. Use Rietveld refinement to quantify CeO2 (fluorite) and BaCeO3 phases; verify absence or <1 wt% of BaCO3. Apply Williamson–Hall analysis to extract volume-weighted crystallite size and microstrain; target BaCeO3 25–33 nm and CeO2 19–35 nm for 800–1000 °C conditions. For polymorph assessment, perform high-temperature XRD on selected powders (room T→1000 °C) to observe BaCeO3 Pmna→Imma→R-3c→Pm-3m transitions; then ex-situ XRD post-quench to assess retention of higher-symmetry features.

Step9: Raman spectroscopy for carbonate and structural fingerprints. Collect spectra with 532 nm excitation, low laser power to avoid heating. Confirm absence of strong carbonate bands (∼1050–1100 cm⁻¹) after 1000 °C treatment. Track CeO2 F2g mode (~465 cm⁻¹) and BaCeO3 characteristic modes to gauge strain (peak positions/widths). Compare rapid-cool vs slow-cool to detect differences indicative of frozen-in strain or polymorph signatures.

Step10: Morphology and chemistry (powder). Examine by SEM for agglomerate size; if available, perform TEM/SAED on representative samples to directly measure primary crystallite sizes and assess BaCeO3/CeO2 heterointerfaces. Use EDS to verify Ba and Ce distribution and check for secondary reaction layers.

Step11: Select optimal nanoparticle batches. Choose compositions meeting: (i) dual-phase BaCeO3+CeO2 with desired ratio (r-dependent); (ii) crystallite sizes within ≤35 nm; (iii) no detectable BaCO3 by XRD and Raman; (iv) significant microstrain difference between rapid-cool and slow-cool batches (for stress tuning evaluation). Retain both rapid-cool and slow-cool powders for film trials.

Step12: Formulate REBCO precursor inks with nanoparticles. Use a well-established CSD route (e.g., TFA-MOD or fluorine-free metal-organic) compatible with IBAD-MgO-buffered Hastelloy tapes. Disperse selected nanopowders into the REBCO precursor solution at 1, 3, 5, 8 vol% relative to final film volume. Achieve stable dispersions by sequential ultrasonication (bath then probe) and bead milling (0.1–0.3 mm zirconia media); add a minimal amount of compatible dispersant (e.g., acetic/propionic acid) if needed; keep water content low. Measure viscosity and zeta potential; target no visible sedimentation over 24 h.

Step13: Substrate preparation and deposition. Use 1–3 cm coupons of IBAD-MgO-based buffered Hastelloy (e.g., Y2O3/YSZ/CeO2/MgO stack). Clean by solvent rinse and UV-ozone or mild plasma. Deposit nanoparticle-laden REBCO ink by spin coating (e.g., 2000–3000 rpm, 30–60 s) or slot-die for uniform films aiming for ~0.5–1 μm final thickness after full conversion (multiple coats as needed, with intermediate pyrolysis).

Step14: Pyrolysis and REBCO conversion heat treatment. Execute a standard CSD thermal schedule tuned to the chosen chemistry: (i) dry at 120–150 °C to remove solvents; (ii) pyrolyze 250–450 °C in humid O2/N2 to decompose organics; (iii) crystallize REBCO at 750–800 °C for 30–90 min in low pO2 (∼100–300 ppm O2 in N2) to promote epitaxial growth; (iv) implement the stress-tuning rapid cooling: cool from crystallization temperature at 10 °C/min to 450 °C; hold at 450 °C in O2 for oxygenation 1–2 h; then cool to room temperature. Prepare matched controls with slow cooling (2 °C/min) from the crystallization step.

Step15: Structural and textural characterization of films. Perform XRD θ–2θ to confirm c-axis oriented REBCO; obtain rocking curve (Δω) and φ-scan (Δφ) to assess biaxial texture retention (targets Δω ≤ 3°, Δφ ≤ 7°, comparable to undoped films). Look for BaCeO3/CeO2 reflections and assess their orientation distribution. Use Williamson–Hall or line-broadening methods cautiously for nanoparticle-containing films to estimate microstrain. Prepare FIB cross-sections for SEM to determine film thickness, nanoparticle distribution, and interfaces; perform EDS line scans/maps for Ba and Ce to confirm inclusion localization and absence of reaction layers. If available, do TEM/STEM for direct imaging of nanoparticle size, spacing, and interface coherency.

Step16: Verify absence of carbonate and interfacial cleanliness in films. Acquire Raman spectra on films (532 nm) to ensure no carbonate signatures; cross-check with XRD for BaCO3 peaks. Examine interfaces in FIB-TEM for any secondary reaction layers; if detected, adjust pyrolysis or base synthesis washing to further reduce carbon residue.

Step17: Electrical and superconducting characterization. Measure resistivity vs temperature (R–T) to determine Tc onset and zero resistance; aim for Tc ≥ 90 K (depending on RE). Perform transport Jc measurements using four-probe method with 1 μV/cm criterion at: (i) 77 K, self-field; (ii) 30–65 K in magnetic fields up to 9–14 T (as available), for H∥c and H∥ab; (iii) angular dependence Jc(θ) at fixed fields (e.g., 1, 3, 5 T) to assess pinning anisotropy. Complement with magnetization-based Jc via VSM and Bean model for cross-validation. Record E–J curves to extract n-values.

Step18: Pinning force analysis and microstructure–property correlation. From Jc(B) data, compute pinning force density Fp = μ0 Jc B; scale Fp/Fp,max vs reduced field b to identify dominant pinning mechanisms and compare rapid-cool vs slow-cool and varying nanoparticle loadings. Correlate Fp,max and Jc enhancements with nanoparticle size/distribution, microstrain (from W–H), and BaCeO3 polymorph/strain indicators (Raman/XRD). Assess whether rapid-cool samples exhibit higher Fp consistent with added strain fields.

Step19: Parametric matrix and controls. For each nanoparticle loading (1, 3, 5, 8 vol%) and Ce/Ba ratio (r = 1.0, 1.2, 1.5), process films under both cooling protocols. Include three controls: (i) REBCO without nanoparticles; (ii) REBCO + CeO2-only nanoparticles (commercial or synthesized analogously without Ba); (iii) REBCO + BaCeO3-only nanoparticles (synthesized at r = 1.0 with processing tuned to maximize BaCeO3 content). Maintain identical deposition and heat-treatment conditions across sets.

Step20: Acceptance criteria and decision gates. Proceed with in-field testing for samples meeting: (i) nanoparticle sizes ≤35 nm in film cross-sections; (ii) no detectable BaCO3 by film Raman/XRD; (iii) texture not degraded relative to control (Δω, Δφ within 10% of baseline); (iv) Tc within 2 K of control; (v) Jc(77 K, self-field) ≥90% of control; (vi) at 30–65 K and 1–5 T, at least 20–50% Jc enhancement over control for best candidates. Use these to select optimal Ce/Ba ratio and loading.

Step21: Troubleshooting and optimization. If BaCO3 appears, further reduce CO2 exposure in Steps 2–5 and increase post-precipitation washing; consider brief 700 °C pre-calcination under dry O2 to remove traces before final calcine. If nanoparticles agglomerate in ink, adjust solvent polarity, add a small amount of non-ionic dispersant compatible with MOD, increase bead milling time, or perform surface hydroxylation by mild H2O2 treatment. If texture degrades, reduce nanoparticle loading, lower ink viscosity, or adjust pyrolysis ramp to prevent pore formation.

Step22: Scale-up test. Apply the optimized nanoparticle dispersion to 10–100 cm tape segments via slot-die coating with web speeds matched to established MOD lines. Repeat Steps 14–18 on segments sampled along length to evaluate uniformity and reproducibility of nanoparticle dispersion and Jc(B,T).

Step23: Documentation and data management. Record all synthesis parameters (pH, addition rates, temperatures), DTA/TG-MS traces, XRD/Raman/SEM data, heat-treatment profiles, and electrical data with traceable sample IDs to enable correlation and reproducibility. Archive raw and processed datasets for subsequent analysis and modeling.

Step24: Optional advanced characterization. For top candidates, perform atom probe tomography or nano-beam diffraction (if available) to probe interface chemistry/strain; conduct in-situ TEM heating experiments on nanoparticles to directly observe BaCeO3 phase transitions and assess metastable phase retention upon quench.

Step25: Final outcome and iteration. Based on correlations and acceptance criteria, converge on one or two nanoparticle compositions and loadings that maximize in-field Jc at target temperatures/fields. Iterate minor adjustments in calcination temperature and cooling rate to fine-tune strain fields. Prepare additional tapes to confirm reproducibility and readiness for application in high-field magnets or fault-current limiters.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1 – Dissolution of CeO₂  
- Place stoichiometric CeO₂ (99.9 %, Crytur) in a beaker, add 1:1 (vol.) diluted HNO₃ (stoichiometric ratio CeO₂:HNO₃ = 1:4.5) and heat the suspension to 80 °C.  
- Add 30 % H₂O₂ (LachNer) drop-wise under continued heating until the solid CeO₂ fully dissolves, forming Ce(III) nitrate solution.

Step 2 – Dissolution of Ba(OH)₂·8H₂O  
- In a separate beaker suspend Ba(OH)₂·8H₂O (p.a., FLUKA) in water.  
- Add concentrated HNO₃ drop-wise until the hydroxide completely dissolves.

Step 3 – Solution mixing and concentration adjustment  
- Combine the two clear solutions and dilute with water to obtain a total cation concentration of 0.1 mol L⁻¹.

Step 4 – Reverse co-precipitation  
- Prepare an aqueous receiver solution containing NH₃ and H₂O₂ (exact concentrations not specified).  
- Add the 0.1 mol L⁻¹ Ba/Ce nitrate solution drop-wise into the NH₃/H₂O₂ receiver under stirring (no further details on addition rate or temperature given).

Step 5 – Precipitate work-up  
- Wash the resulting solid with concentrated aqueous NH₃ (concentration not quantified).  
- Filter, then dry the powder at 110 °C for 12 h.

Step 6 – Heat treatment / crystallisation  
- Place dried powder in a furnace, heat at 10 °C min⁻¹ to either 800 °C or 1000 °C, hold 60 min, then cool rapidly to room temperature.

Step 7 – Characterisation sequence  
- Record simultaneous DTA/TG/MS (heating rate 10 K min⁻¹, flowing air) on the 110 °C-dried precursor.  
- Collect X-ray diffraction (Co Kα, Bruker AXS D2 Phaser, Bragg-Brentano geometry) on as-dried and on annealed powders; analyse phases with HighScore Plus and PDF-4 database; perform Rietveld refinement and Williamson–Hall line-broadening analysis to extract crystallite sizes.  
- Acquire Raman spectra (DXR Microscope, Thermo Scientific; Nd:YAG laser, multichannel CCD) over 0.01–1000 µm range; inspect CeO₂ T₂g band (≈465 cm⁻¹), BaCeO₃ lattice modes (50–400 cm⁻¹) and BaCO₃ symmetric stretch (≈1060 cm⁻¹).  
- Image powder morphology with SEM (Lyra3 GMU FIB-SEM, Tescan).

[Experimental Design Details]
- Precipitation chemistry: avoids carbonate/oxalate precipitants; relies on pH-driven re-oxidation of Ce(III)→CeO₂ and low solubility of Ba(OH)₂ at high pH.  
- Target phases: BaCeO₃ (major) and CeO₂ (inevitable secondary phase because Ba precipitation is incomplete).  
- Annealing temperatures chosen on the basis of DTA/TG CO₂-release feature observed at ≈850 °C.  
- Grain-size evaluation performed only for the two main phases (BaCeO₃ and CeO₂) using the same Williamson–Hall formalism.  
- No further processing (e.g., grinding, sieving, pelletising) is mentioned after heat treatment.

Experiment: Step1: Define objectives and metrics: Target a Gd0.5Yb0.5Ba2Cu3O7-δ (GdYbBCO) coated conductor with hierarchical pinning from self-assembled (011)-BaCuO2 nanorods and (Gd,Yb)2O3 nanodots on identical IBAD-MgO/Hastelloy templates, 0.54 μm superconducting layer, c-axis texture Δω≈2°, in-plane texture Δφ≈4°, c-lattice parameter 11.63–11.67 Å after oxygenation. Verify that Cu/Ba=1.19 at RE/Ba=0.65 maximizes nanorod length/aspect ratio and density, minimizes interfacial misfit (~5.6%), and yields strong Jc vs B performance across 4–77 K. Establish performance metrics: Jc(4 K, 5 T) ≥ 13.2 MA cm⁻² (transport, 1 μV cm⁻¹), α≈0.39 from Jc∝B^−α in the high-field regime, B*≈551 mT at 10 K, Fp,max≈670 GN m⁻³ at 4 K, and Jc(>20 T, 4.2 K) exceeding a 15% Zr-doped benchmark fabricated under comparable conditions.

Step2: Substrate and buffer procurement/QC: Obtain a single production lot of 4–12 mm wide Hastelloy C276 tapes with identical buffer stacks (e.g., amorphous oxide/Y2O3 seed/IBAD-MgO/MgO cap/LaMnO3 or CeO2 cap) providing Δω≈2° and Δφ≈4°. Verify template texture on at least 10 locations per 1 m by XRD rocking curves (002 MgO and cap) and φ-scans (in-plane reflections). Reject any template sections with Δω>3° or Δφ>5°.

Step3: Reel-to-reel MOCVD reactor setup: Use a liquid-delivery MOCVD system with independent heated bubblers for Cu, Ba, Gd, and Yb precursors; carrier gas Ar with O2 co-flow. Set web width to match tape width; use in-situ IR pyrometry for substrate temperature feedback and mass-flow controllers for precursor delivery. Verify uniform substrate heating across web with thermal imaging.

Step4: Metal-organic precursor selection and stock solutions: Use volatile β-diketonate precursors with demonstrated stability for REBCO MOCVD, e.g., Cu(hfac)2·TMEDA (or Cu(tmhd)2 with suitable adduct), Ba(tmhd)2, Gd(tmhd)3, Yb(tmhd)3 dissolved in anhydrous toluene or hexane with stabilizers to prevent hydrolysis. Prepare separate stock solutions; determine concentrations gravimetrically and by ICP-OES to ±2%.

Step5: Delivery calibration: Calibrate precursor molar delivery rates by passing the vapor into a quartz cold finger at deposition setpoints (without substrate), collecting condensate for ICP-OES to determine relative Cu:Ba:Gd:Yb delivery. Adjust bubbler temperatures and carrier flows to achieve target molar feed ratios; repeat until Cu/Ba and (Gd+Yb)/Ba are within ±0.01 of setpoints across a 2 h run.

Step6: Deposition setpoints for GdYbBCO: Set substrate zone temperature 790–810 °C (optimize within this window during initial trials), total reactor pressure 5–15 Torr, oxygen partial pressure 2–6 Torr, Ar balance, web speed tuned to yield 0.54 μm thickness (e.g., 1–5 cm min⁻¹ depending on precursor flux). Use ozone or increased O2 if needed to stabilize c-axis epitaxy; maintain dew point below −40 °C in gas lines. Keep identical setpoints for all samples except Cu/Ba and RE/Ba.

Step7: Oxygenation and cool-down: After growth, cool to 500 °C in 1 atm O2, dwell 1 h, ramp to 450 °C, dwell 2–3 h to fully oxygenate (target δ≈0.1–0.2), then cool to room temperature at 2–5 °C min⁻¹ in O2. Optionally include an in-situ low-temperature O2 soak if reactor allows.

Step8: Thickness and uniformity verification: Measure film thickness by cross-sectional SEM on cleaved or FIB-prepared sections and by profilometry on masked steps; target 0.54±0.03 μm across the width and along 1 m length. Map thickness at 10 cm intervals to assess R2R uniformity.

Step9: Experimental matrix A (Cu/Ba sweep at fixed RE/Ba=0.65): Fabricate five tapes with Cu/Ba=1.15, 1.17, 1.19, 1.20, 1.21 at fixed (Gd+Yb)/Ba=0.65 and Gd:Yb=1:1. For each composition, produce at least 30 cm length; section 5 cm coupons for characterization and retain the rest for electrical testing.

Step10: Experimental matrix B (RE/Ba sweep at fixed Cu/Ba=1.19): Fabricate five tapes with RE/Ba=0.55, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70, 0.75 at fixed Cu/Ba=1.19 and Gd:Yb=1:1. Maintain identical deposition parameters; collect similar coupon sets.

Step11: Reference benchmark (optional but recommended): Fabricate a 15% Zr-doped REBCO reference on identical templates and thickness using the same MOCVD tool (e.g., add Zr(tmhd)4 to generate BaZrO3 nanorods) to serve as a performance baseline under identical measurement protocols.

Step12: Phase purity and texture (XRD): Perform θ–2θ scans (20–70° 2θ, Cu Kα) to confirm c-axis oriented REBCO (00l) peaks and absence/minimization of unwanted phases (e.g., CuO, RECuO2). Extract c-lattice parameter from 00l peaks using Nelson–Riley correction; accept 11.63–11.67 Å. Measure rocking curves (ω) of REBCO 005 for Δω and φ-scans of 103 for Δφ; accept Δω<3°, Δφ<5° for all samples.

Step13: 2D-XRD for secondary phase orientation: Use area detector with sample tilt χ≈45° and azimuthal scans to detect (011)-BaCuO2 oriented features and (Gd,Yb)2O3 reflections. Quantify intensity along c-axis vs off-axis to assess vertical alignment of BCO nanorods and layering of REO nanodots. Compare integrated intensities across compositions.

Step14: Surface morphology and precipitates (SEM/EDS): Image surfaces at multiple magnifications to detect CuO/RECuO2 precipitates. Use EDS point and map scans to identify precipitate composition. Expect minimal surface precipitates at Cu/Ba=1.19 and increased precipitates at Cu/Ba≥1.20; document areal coverage as a function of Cu/Ba.

Step15: Cross-sectional TEM sample preparation: Prepare plan-view and cross-section lamellae by focused ion beam (final polish ≤2 keV to minimize damage) at positions centered across the tape width. For each sample, prepare at least two cross-sectional lamellae to ensure statistical significance.

Step16: STEM imaging and EDS/EELS: Acquire HAADF-STEM images along [100]/[010] zone axes to visualize BaCuO2 nanorods and REO nanodots. Perform STEM-EDS maps (Ba, Cu, Gd, Yb, O) to identify phase chemistry. For each sample, count and measure ≥100 BaCuO2 nanorods (diameter, length, spacing) and ≥100 REO nanodots (size, layer spacing, tilt angle relative to ab-plane). Calculate nanorod density (per μm²), aspect ratio, and nanodot areal density.

Step17: Strain mapping and interface assessment: Acquire high-resolution TEM images across BCO/REBCO interfaces and perform geometric phase analysis (GPA) to map in-plane and out-of-plane strain. Extract average tensile strain in BCO and compressive strain in the matrix near interfaces; document presence or absence of periodic misfit dislocations. Define “coherent” as absence of a regular dislocation array over ≥20 nm of interface.

Step18: Lattice mismatch calculation: Using measured lattice parameters (from XRD for REBCO and literature/DFT-informed values for BaCuO2 adjusted by observed strain), compute the lattice mismatch along relevant matching directions for (011)-BCO//c-axis REBCO using f=(d_inclusion−d_matrix)/d_matrix. Track how f changes with Cu/Ba and RE/Ba and correlate with observed interface coherence and nanorod continuity.

Step19: Texture uniformity along length: On each tape, perform XRD rocking curves at 0, 15, 30 cm to verify Δω and Δφ uniformity; document any drift. Only proceed with electrical tests on sections meeting the texture criteria.

Step20: Electrical bridge patterning and contacts: Define 0.5–1.0 mm wide, 10–15 mm long bridges via UV laser scribing or mechanical scribing through the superconducting layer to isolate tracks. Deposit a thin Ag cap (0.5–1 μm) by sputtering if not already present; attach four contacts with Ag-filled epoxy and anneal at 200 °C for 10–20 min in O2. Verify contact resistance <100 μΩ at 300 K.

Step21: Transport Ic/Jc measurements (0–5 T): Measure Ic at 77 K, self-field to screen samples; then at 4.2, 10, 20, 30, 40, 65, 77 K in applied magnetic fields 0–5 T using a split-pair or vector magnet and low-noise current source. Use a 1 μV cm⁻¹ electric field criterion. Mount on a rotator and measure Ic(θ) from 0–180° in 5–10° steps at representative fields (e.g., 1, 3, 5 T). Record voltage–current curves to assess n-values; compute Jc from cross-section (thickness from Step8).

Step22: Magnetization Jc (up to 14 T): On unpatterned coupons, measure M(H) loops at 4.2, 10, 20, 30, 40, 65, 77 K up to 14 T with field both parallel to c and parallel to ab. Convert to Jc using the Bean model for rectangular geometry; calibrate the Bean-derived Jc against transport Jc at overlapping fields (e.g., 1–5 T) to ensure consistency and correct for geometric factors.

Step23: High-field transport (>20 T): Send selected optimal and control samples (e.g., Cu/Ba=1.19 at RE/Ba=0.65; Cu/Ba extremes; RE/Ba extremes; Zr-doped reference) to a high-field facility with resistive or hybrid magnets. Measure Ic(B) up to 31–35 T at 4.2 K for B∥c and B∥ab over the same 1 μV cm⁻¹ criterion and identical bridge design. Ensure low thermal gradients and use pulsed-current or steady-state with thermal monitoring to avoid Joule heating.

Step24: Data reduction and metrics: Derive Jc(B,T,θ) surfaces for all samples. Fit high-field Jc(B) to a power law to extract α for B∥c and B∥ab; compute the pinning force density Fp=Jc·B and determine Fp,max and the corresponding field. Determine B* (depinning or characteristic field) using Kramer plots or the field at which Fp reaches 25% of Fp,max, and compare across compositions. Extract anisotropy ratio Jc(B∥ab)/Jc(B∥c). Plot angular Jc peaks to assess c-axis and ab-plane correlated pinning contributions.

Step25: Correlation analysis: Correlate Cu/Ba with (i) BaCuO2 nanorod length, diameter, density, (ii) presence of CuO/RECuO2 precipitates, (iii) interface coherence and strain, and (iv) α and Jc minima. Correlate RE/Ba with REO nanodot density and layering, BaCuO2 nanorod morphology, and resulting ab-plane pinning and Fp. Identify the composition that minimizes mismatch (near 5.6%), maximizes nanorod continuity, maintains dense layered REO nanodots with ≤7° tilt, and optimizes Jc and Fp across T and B.

Step26: Validate interface tuning: From GPA and HRTEM, quantify frequency (per μm) of interfacial misfit dislocations at BCO/REBCO for each composition. Plot dislocation density versus calculated mismatch; verify that deviation from Cu/Ba=1.19 or RE/Ba=0.65 increases mismatch (toward ~6.6%), introduces dislocations, and correlates with shortened rods and degraded α. Confirm that the optimal composition exhibits coherent, dislocation-free interfaces over the longest rod lengths.

Step27: Texture dependence check: Confirm that texture (Δω, Δφ) remains invariant across composition series and that variations in nanorod alignment (from 2D-XRD and TEM tilt distributions) are not substrate-driven. Quantify nanorod tilt dispersion and relate to Δω/Δφ to support the texture tuning hypothesis.

Step28: Stress/strain role: Using GPA strain maps and elastic constants from literature, estimate local elastic strain in BCO and REBCO near interfaces across compositions. Confirm that elastic strain is accommodated without plastic relaxation (no dislocation arrays) at the optimum and that this correlates with longer, continuous nanorods aligned along c.

Step29: Long-length uniformity and scale-up: On the optimal composition tape, map Ic(77 K, self-field) and Ic(4.2 K, 3 T) every 5–10 cm over 1 m. Perform XRD c-parameter and texture checks at several positions. Use portable XRF or WDXRF to map Cu/Ba and RE/Ba along length; acceptance criteria ±0.01 in ratios and ±5% in Ic. If needed, adjust R2R process (web speed, precursor flows) and repeat.

Step30: Mechanical and thermal robustness: Subject the optimal tape to 100 thermal cycles between 300 K and 4.2 K in helium; measure Ic at 4.2 K, 3 T and at 77 K, self-field every 10 cycles. Perform bend tests around 20–30 mm diameter mandrels; measure Ic before/after to assess strain tolerance. Document any performance degradation.

Step31: Benchmark comparison: Measure and analyze the 15% Zr-doped reference in the same setups to compare Jc(B,T,θ), α, Fp,max, and B* with the optimal GdYbBCO composition. Confirm whether the optimized hierarchical pinning architecture surpasses the Zr-doped baseline above 20 T at 4.2 K.

Step32: Risk management and controls: Monitor precursor purity by NMR/GC-MS quarterly; replace if degradation is detected. Periodically re-calibrate delivery (Step5). Use the same IBAD lot across samples; if a new lot is required, re-qualify texture. Implement oxygen partial pressure and substrate temperature alarms in MOCVD to prevent drift. For TEM statistics, blind the analyst to composition to minimize bias.

Step33: Safety and handling: Follow standard safety protocols for handling metal-organic precursors (air/moisture sensitivity), high-temperature MOCVD operation, focused ion beam preparation, cryogenic measurements, and high-field facility requirements. Ensure proper ventilation, PPE, and gas monitoring.

Step34: Documentation and data management: Record all deposition parameters (flows, temperatures, pressures, web speed), oxygenation profiles, sample identifiers, and measurement conditions. Store raw and processed data (XRD, SEM/TEM, EDS/GPA, transport, magnetization) with metadata for reproducibility. Prepare a decision matrix linking composition, microstructure, and performance to guide subsequent optimization cycles.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1: Substrate preparation  
- Use a single 65 µm-thick, 12 mm-wide Hastelloy tape carrying a pre-deposited IBAD-MgO buffer stack: Hastelloy/Al₂O₃/Y₂O₃/IBAD-MgO/MgO/LaMnO₃.  
- Confirm buffer in-plane texture uniformity: XRD φ-scan FWHM of LMO(110) = 6.3° ± 0.2°.

Step 2: Precursor solution preparation  
- Dissolve tetramethylheptanedionate complexes of Gd, Yb, Ba and Cu in tetrahydrofuran at designed molar ratios.  
- Keep Gd:Yb = 1:1 in all solutions.

Step 3: MOCVD deposition (reel-to-reel)  
- Chamber pressure: 2.0 Torr.  
- O₂ partial pressure: 0.7 Torr.  
- Substrate temperature: ~775 °C.  
- Deposition rate: ~90 nm min⁻¹.  
- Target film thickness: ~0.54 µm (0.5–0.6 µm verified by TEM).  
- Grow all samples in a single run to ensure identical hardware configuration.

Step 4: Composition series (two independent sets)  
Set-A (Cu/Ba variation, RE/Ba fixed at 1.3:2 in precursor)  
- Precursor Cu/Ba (2Cu:Ba): 2.30, 2.34, 2.38, 2.42 → film labels S2.30, S2.34, S2.38, S2.42.  
Set-B (RE/Ba variation, Cu/Ba fixed at 2.38:2 in precursor)  
- Precursor (GdYb):Ba: 1.1:2, 1.2:2, 1.3:2, 1.4:2, 1.5:2 → film labels S1.1, S1.2, S1.3, S1.4, S1.5.  
- Replicate depositions: ≥3 short samples per composition.

Step 5: Composition verification  
- Measure final film metal ratios by energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS); values listed in Table 1 of the paper.

Step 6: Microstructural characterization  
- X-ray diffraction (Rigaku Smartlab 9000 W, HyPix-3000 detector): θ–2θ scans, ω-scans (005), φ-scans (103), 2D-XRD at χ = 45°.  
- Scanning electron microscopy (JEOL JSM-7001F): surface morphology.  
- Transmission electron microscopy (JEOL JEM-2100F): cross-sectional and plan-view images; selected-area electron diffraction (SAED).  
- Statistical analysis of defect parameters (≥100 BaCuO₂ rods, ≥5 regions per sample): length, cross-sectional width, spacing, splay angle; RE₂O₃ particle size, layer thickness, tilt angle.

Step 7: Transport critical current measurements  
- Cut 1 mm-wide bridges by laser engraving.  
- Four-probe transport Ic at 4–77 K, 0–5 T, electric-field criterion 1 µV cm⁻¹.  
- Measure angular Ic(θ) from θ = 0° (B//c) to 180° in 1 T (77 K), 3 T (65 K, 40 K, 20 K).  
- Extract Jc vs B at θ = 0° and 90°.

Step 8: Magnetometry (representative sample)  
- Magnetization hysteresis loops at 4 K up to 14 T in Quantum Design PPMS.  
- Calculate Jc from loops using Bean model; calibrate against transport Jc at (4 K, 5 T).

Step 9: Data analysis  
- Fit high-field Jc(B) to power law Jc ∝ B^(−α); determine accommodation field B* where Jc(B*) = 0.9 Jc(0).  
- Compute pinning force density Fp = Jc × B.  
- Extract angular minimum Jc_min at 3 T versus temperature.

[Experimental Design Details]
- All depositions use the same buffered substrate tape to eliminate buffer variability.  
- Precursor ratios are converted to film ratios via EDS; small deviations are reported (Table 1).  
- No post-annealing steps are mentioned.  
- TEM sample preparation method not described.  
- Error bars on Jc(77 K, 0 T) come from 3–6 samples per composition.
