Experiment: Step1: Define substrate and buffer architecture: Use 12 mm-wide Hastelloy C-276 tapes with a standard IBAD-based buffer stack (e.g., Al2O3/Y2O3 diffusion barrier, IBAD-MgO template, homo-epitaxial MgO, LaMnO3 cap). Verify initial buffer texture by XRD φ-scan (MgO(220)/LMO(103) FWHM ≤ 5°) and ω-scan (≤ 2°). Clean tape surface reel-to-reel with solvent wipe and low-power O2 plasma to remove organics.
Step2: Prepare PLD targets and calibrations: Fabricate a dense EuBa2Cu3O7-δ target (Eu:Ba:Cu stoichiometric) and a BaHfO3 target. For multi-plume operation, mount two EuBCO targets and one BHO target. Confirm target compositions by XRF/ICP-OES. Pre-condition targets by 10–20 min ablation at process O2 to stabilize plume. Calibrate individual ablation rates (nm/pulse) at set laser fluence and spot size using witness substrates and profilometry.
Step3: Configure MPMT-PLD deposition: Use a multi-plume, multi-turn reel-to-reel PLD system with synchronized beam steering over targets and tape. Set laser repetition to 300 Hz; pulse energy 700–1000 mJ; spot size 2–3 mm² to keep fluence in the 1–3 J/cm² range at each target. Set process O2 to 800–1000 mTorr with high-flow control. Set heater setpoint 1000–1100 °C (calibrated to yield ~optimal REBCO growth; maintain identical setpoint history across runs). Implement tape speed and multi-turn path to achieve an effective deposition rate of 0.2–0.4 µm/min for EuBCO+BHO. Monitor heater backside temperature and tape frontside pyrometry if available.
Step4: Establish BHO doping control (6 mol% in film): Use synchronized plume time-sharing or concurrent ablation to maintain a EuBCO:BHO pulse ratio that yields 6 mol% BHO incorporation (based on prior calibration runs analyzed by XRF/RBS). Implement closed-loop correction: after every 5–10 m of tape, sample a 5 cm section for XRF to verify Hf content; adjust BHO pulse duty cycle by ±1–2% if Hf deviates by >0.5 mol%.
Step5: Multi-cycle thickness build to 3.3 µm with step-wise heater schedule: Divide growth into 4 cycles (e.g., 0.8 µm + 0.8 µm + 0.8 µm + 0.9 µm). For Cycle 1 (near buffer): use lowest setpoint in window (e.g., 1000–1020 °C) to maximize c-axis template quality and minimize a-axis grains. For Cycles 2–4: increase setpoint stepwise by +10–20 °C per cycle to compensate for surface cooling under high flux and to tune adatom mobility. Within each cycle, apply a mild dynamic ramp (+5–10 °C over the cycle) to suppress a-axis formation as the surface roughens. Maintain O2 constant. Keep deposition rate constant initially; for Cycles 3–4 slightly increase BHO pulse fraction (e.g., +5–10% relative pulses) or modestly reduce substrate temperature within the allowed window to promote higher splay in later layers, building a 3-D pinning web.
Step6: Inter-cycle thermal management and stress relaxation: After each growth cycle, ramp to 500–550 °C in 200–500 Torr O2 for 15–30 min to partially oxygenate and smooth the surface via limited diffusion. Cool to ≤200 °C in O2, then to room temperature if required for tape handling. This intermittent cycling relieves cumulative stress; log tape curvature visually and with in-line optical flatness sensors if available.
Step7: Final oxygenation: After the last cycle, perform an ex-situ oxygenation anneal: ramp to 450–500 °C in flowing 1 bar O2, hold 60–120 min, then slow cool at 3–5 °C/min to room temperature in O2. Aim for orthorhombic ordering with Tc near 97 K and ΔTc ≤ 1 K. If Tc onset <95 K or ΔTc >1 K, repeat a 350–400 °C oxygenation soak for 1–2 h and re-check.
Step8: Thickness and morphology verification: Measure film thickness by cross-sectional SEM at several positions and by stylus profilometry across patterned steps on short witness coupons co-deposited with the tape. Target 3.3 ± 0.1 µm total. Record surface roughness (AFM on witness coupons) and correlate with a-axis incidence.
Step9: Phase purity and texture by XRD: Perform θ–2θ scans to confirm c-axis-oriented EuBCO and BHO secondary phase peaks. Extract c-axis lattice parameter using Nelson–Riley extrapolation; target c ≈ 11.73 Å. Measure (005) rocking curve ω-scan; acceptance FWHM ≤ 1.5–1.7°. Measure (103) φ-scan; acceptance FWHM ≤ 2.0–2.3°. Conduct high-order peak analysis for Williamson–Hall micro-strain; target increase from baseline ≤ 0.05% across 1.1 to 3.3 µm. Map texture every 10 m along a 100 m section to assess uniformity.
Step10: Composition and depth profiling: Use XRF for Hf areal density and Eu:Ba:Cu ratios; confirm 6 ± 0.5 mol% BHO. If available, perform RBS or ToF-SIMS on coupons to confirm Hf depth uniformity and identify any BHO-free layers; quantify Hf fluctuations >10% and adjust cycle parameters accordingly.
Step11: Cross-sectional (S)TEM and EDS: Prepare FIB lamellae at bottom, middle, and top locations of the 3.3 µm film. Use STEM-HAADF to image BHO nanocolumns and nanoparticles; measure column diameter (target 3–8 nm), spacing, and splay angle distribution relative to c-axis. Compute splay histograms for each depth; target broadening from bottom (near-vertical) to top (0–20° distribution). Identify and quantify BHO-free layered regions (areal fraction per depth). Use EDS maps to verify Hf-rich columns and detect Cu–O particles and their relation to misoriented EuBCO grains.
Step12: Grain orientation mapping: Quantify a-axis grains and misoriented c-axis grains by plan-view TEM selected area diffraction or precession electron diffraction; alternatively, perform EBSD on polished cross-sections if pattern quality permits. Target a-axis fraction <3–5%. Identify low-angle grain boundaries associated with Cu–O particles; document misorientation distributions and boundary densities.
Step13: Electrical ρ(T) characterization: Pattern 2–3 mm long, 0.5–1 mm wide bridges on short tape sections by laser scribing. Deposit Ag pads (sputter/evaporate) and anneal at 200–250 °C in O2 for contact. Measure ρ(T) from 300 K to 10 K in PPMS (≤1 mA to avoid self-heating). Determine Tc onset and ΔTc (10–90% criterion). Record normal-state ρ(300 K) and RRR; re-oxygenate if ΔTc >1 K or RRR anomalous.
Step14: Magnetization Jc via VSM/SQUID: Cut 3×3 mm² squares and measure M(H) loops at 5, 30, 77 K up to 7 T with field along c and ab. Extract Jc using the Bean model. Use these data to pre-screen before high-field transport, and to estimate Jc(B) scaling exponents.
Step15: High-field transport Jc(B,θ): Pattern 1–2 mm wide bridges; verify uniform cross-section by microscopy. Use four-probe configuration, 1 µV/cm electric field criterion. Measure at 77 K self-field; at 30 K, 5 T with full angular rotation (0–180°, 5° steps); and at 4.2 K up to 18 T (B//c and angular). Record Jc anisotropy ratio Jc,max/Jc,min at 30 K, 5 T; target <1.2. At 4.2 K, 14 T (B//c) target ~5 MA/cm²; verify reduced Jc(B) decay compared to 1.1 µm control.
Step16: Angular pinning analysis: Fit Jc(θ) using mixed correlated/random pinning models (e.g., summation of c-axis, ab-plane, and isotropic components with splay-induced broadening). Correlate splay distributions from STEM with angular widths in Jc(θ). Examine matching or crossover fields and temperature dependence (4.2–40 K).
Step17: Controls and thickness series: Prepare control tapes: (a) 1.1 µm EuBCO+6% BHO with identical settings; (b) 3.3 µm EuBCO without BHO; (c) 3.3 µm EuBCO+6% BHO grown in a single continuous cycle (no step-wise T changes). Repeat Steps 9–15. Compare texture, micro-strain, splay, and Jc(B,θ) to isolate the effects of multi-cycle splaying and tolerated misorientation.
Step18: Process-structure-property iteration: If a-axis fraction >5% or ω-FWHM >1.8°, increase within-cycle temperature ramps by +5 °C and reduce deposition rate 10–15% in early cycles. If Jc self-field at 77 K drops below 1.2 MA/cm² while in-field gains are modest, reduce Cu–O supersaturation by slightly higher substrate temperature (+10 °C) and/or lower PLD fluence in the first two cycles to suppress misoriented nucleation. If splay angles are too small (<5° at top), increase BHO pulse fraction by 5% in the last cycle or lower the last-cycle temperature by 10–15 °C (keeping within epitaxial window) to limit adatom diffusion and promote splay.
Step19: Residual stress and integrity: Use Williamson–Hall from multiple Bragg orders to estimate micro-strain in as-grown vs post-oxygenation states; target ≤0.25% at 3.3 µm. Check for through-thickness cracks by cross-sectional SEM/TEM. Perform reel-to-reel bend testing (e.g., down to 15–20 mm radius) and measure Jc retention at 77 K, self-field; target ≥95% retention after 100 cycles. If cracking observed, lengthen inter-cycle holds and reduce final cycle thickness by ~0.1–0.2 µm.
Step20: Uniformity and scale-up: Deposit 100 m tape with the optimized recipe. Sample 10 cm sections every 10 m. Perform rapid XRD ω/φ, XRF for Hf%, and 77 K self-field Ic mapping (non-contact scanning Hall or transport on 2 mm strips) to check uniformity (±10%). Spot-check 30 K, 5 T Jc(θ) at head, middle, tail. Evaluate reproducibility across two production runs.
Step21: Data integration and acceptance criteria: Accept batch if (a) c-axis parameter ≈ 11.73 Å and Tc = 96–98 K with ΔTc ≤ 0.8 K; (b) ω-FWHM ≤ 1.6° and φ-FWHM ≤ 2.1°; (c) a-axis fraction ≤ 3%; (d) micro-strain ≤ 0.25%; (e) 77 K self-field Jc ≥ 1.3 MA/cm²; (f) 4.2 K, 14 T Jc (B//c) ≥ 4.5–5.0 MA/cm²; (g) 30 K, 5 T anisotropy ratio ≤ 1.2. If any metric fails, apply Step18 adjustments and re-run on short test tapes.
Step22: Optional advanced characterization: Perform small-angle X-ray scattering on coupons to statistically quantify nanoparticle size distributions; conduct electron tomography on selected lamellae to reconstruct 3D nanocolumn networks and splay. If available, perform synchrotron XRD sin²ψ to cross-check residual stress. Use ToF-SIMS to examine oxygen stoichiometry gradients through thickness.
Step23: Documentation and safety: Maintain detailed run logs (laser energy, pulse counts per target, O2 pressure, heater setpoints per cycle, tape speed). Enforce laser and high-O2 safety protocols; handle Hf-containing powders with appropriate PPE and HEPA-equipped hoods. Archive all raw and processed data for traceability and future optimization.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1: Substrate provision  
- Start from commercial buffered tapes: C276 / Al₂O₃ / Y₂O₃ / IBAD-MgO / LaMnO₃ / CeO₂ (no further substrate processing described).

Step 2: Target preparation  
- Use one 6 mol % BaHfO₃-doped EuBCO sintered target (no target fabrication details given).

Step 3: Reel-to-reel MPMT-PLD deposition  
- Mount the buffered tape in the industrial MPMT-PLD system equipped with a LEAP-300 K excimer laser and planar heater.  
- Set oxygen partial pressure 800–1000 mTorr, deposition temperature 1000–1100 °C, laser repetition rate 300 Hz, single-pulse energy 700–1000 mJ.  
- Raise the set temperature as the number of deposition cycles increases to counteract surface cooling.  
- Run 1 cycle for S1 (≈1.1 µm) and 3 sequential cycles for S2 (≈3.3 µm); no other parameter change is specified.

Step 4: Structural characterisation  
- X-ray diffraction (Bruker D8 ADVANCE, Cu-Kα): θ–2θ (5–60°), ω-scan on (005), φ-scan on (103); calculate c-axis lattice parameter (Nelson–Riley) and c-axis micro-strain (Williamson–Hall).  
- Cross-sectional TEM: prepare lamellae by Ga-ion FIB (TESCAN GAIA3); inspect in Talos F200X TEM at 200 kV; record bright-field and STEM images and perform EDS mapping (O, Eu, Cu, Ba, Hf).

Step 5: Superconducting property measurement  
- Resistivity ρ(T): four-probe method in Quantum Design PPMS under selected magnetic fields; determine Tc (50 % ρn drop) and extract irreversibility field Birr from dρ/dT peak.  
- Critical current density Jc(B): measure magnetic hysteresis loops (PPMS) and apply Bean model; obtain Jc at 77 K, 4.2 K, 30 K, 50 K in perpendicular field (B // c).  
- Angular Jc(θ): micro-bridge 50 µm wide patterned by 1095 nm, 20 W pulsed fibre laser; four-probe transport in 18 T cryostat (Tohoku Univ.) with 1 µV cm⁻¹ criterion at 30 K, 5 T and 50 K, 3 T.

[Experimental Design Details]
- Samples: two final tapes, S1 (1.1 µm) and S2 (3.3 µm) EuBCO layers on identical buffered substrates; no post-annealing or oxygenation step is mentioned.  
- Deposition parameters are kept inside the ranges above; exact values for each cycle are not tabulated.  
- Temperature adjustment protocol: increase set temperature with cycle number—no quantitative ramp profile provided.  
- Micro-bridge fabrication: laser patterning conditions (power, pulse duration, scan speed) apart from wavelength and nominal power are not specified.  
- Data analysis: Bean model for Jc from magnetisation; Birr fitted to Birr ∝ [1 – (T/Tc)]^β; Jc(B) curves analysed for crossover field H* (90 % of self-field Jc) and power-law exponent α.

Aim to fabricate 1 μm thick EuBa2Cu3O7-δ (EuBCO) films on reel-to-reel IBAD-MgO templates with embedded BaSnxHf1-xO3 (BSHO) nanocolumns (~5 nm diameter, ~2200 μm−2 density) aligned along c-axis using multi-plume multi-turn PLD, targeting: (a) c-lattice parameter ≈ 11.744 Å, (b) in-plane texture Δφ ≈ 2.6°, out-of-plane texture Δω ≈ 1.5°, (c) microstrain ≈ 0.29%, and (d) high in-field Jc with non-saturating Fp up to ≥24 T at low T. Design a sample set including: (i) co-doped series with total APC content 8 mol% and varying BSO:BHO ratios (6:2, 5:3, 4.5:3.5, 4:4, 3:5); (ii) single-dopant controls at 8 mol% BSO-only and 8 mol% BHO-only; (iii) growth-rate series (20, 50, 100, 150 nm s−1); (iv) thickness series (0.5, 1.0, 1.5 μm); (v) oxygenation series; and (vi) texture variation using different IBAD templates if available.

Step2: Prepare and qualify IBAD templates. Use commercially available Hastelloy-coated tapes with standard buffer stack (e.g., Y2O3/YSZ/CeO2 or LaMnO3/CeO2 over IBAD-MgO). Verify biaxial texture on coupons cut from the reel: φ scans on MgO {220} and cap layer {111}/{200} to confirm Δφ ≤ 3°; ω-rocking curves Δω ≤ 2°. Clean tape surfaces with solvent rinse (acetone/isopropanol), dry nitrogen blow, and brief low-energy oxygen plasma (<50 W, 30 s) to remove organic residues without damaging buffers.

Step3: Fabricate PLD targets. Prepare dense ceramic targets: (a) EuBCO stoichiometric target with slight Cu excess (≤1 mol%) to stabilize phase at high rate; (b) BSO target; (c) BHO target. Sinter targets to ≥95% density to ensure stable ablation. Confirm phase purity by XRD and bulk composition by ICP-OES. Lap faces to uniform roughness and precondition by ablating ≥10,000 pulses before use.

Step4: Configure the multi-plume multi-turn (MPMT) PLD line. Arrange separate plumes for EuBCO, BSO, and BHO along the web path in a high-uniformity chamber with substrate heating (radiant or laser) capable of 750–820 °C at the tape surface. Equip with multiple synchronized high-repetition-rate lasers (e.g., 355/248/266 nm) delivering 1.5–2.0 J cm−2 fluence at the target, repetition 200–1000 Hz per plume to reach >100 nm s−1 effective growth. Implement reel-to-reel transport with multiple passes (turns) through the plumes. Integrate pyrometry for true tape temperature, in-line optical emission monitoring for plume stability, and residual gas analysis for pO2 control.

Step5: Calibrate single-plume ablation rates. On stationary single-crystal substrates (LaAlO3 or SrTiO3) and short IBAD tape coupons, measure deposition per pulse for each target at fixed laser parameters via X-ray reflectivity (XRR) or profilometry (lift-off masks). Determine: (a) EuBCO thickness per pulse (t_EBCO), (b) BSO and BHO equivalent thickness per pulse (t_BSO, t_BHO). Repeat at several substrate temperatures and pO2 to map rate dependence.

Step6: Calibrate co-deposition flux ratios. In a static coupon configuration, interleave pulses (or web dwell times) from EuBCO, BSO, and BHO plumes to achieve 3.5 mol% BHO + 4.5 mol% BSO relative to EuBCO. Use the measured t_EBCO, t_BSO, t_BHO to compute required pulse ratios or dwell times. Verify film composition by XRF on large-area coupons and by ICP-OES on sacrificial scraped films. Target ±0.3 mol% accuracy for each dopant.

Step7: Determine growth window for vertical BSHO column formation. On single-crystal and IBAD coupons, perform a small parameter sweep of substrate temperature (770–810 °C) and oxygen partial pressure (100–300 mTorr) at moderate growth rate (~50 nm s−1) with the 4.5:3.5 BSO:BHO pulse ratio. Use cross-sectional TEM on 2–3 conditions to confirm columnar versus particulate morphology and preliminary diameters. Select conditions that yield vertically aligned nanocolumns with minimal lateral coarsening.

Step8: Scale to ultra-high growth rates. Increase repetition rate and web speed to reach target growth rates (≥100 nm s−1). Keep the same temperature and pO2 from Step7. Use a multi-turn path so that each pass deposits ~100–200 nm to maintain texture and column alignment; complete 5–10 turns for ~1 μm total. After each pass, maintain temperature and pO2 to avoid thermal cycling.

Step9: In-situ cool-down and oxygenation. After the final pass, raise pO2 to 300–500 mTorr, dwell at deposition temperature for 2–5 min to allow surface equilibration, then cool at 5–10 °C min−1 to 450–500 °C while increasing O2 to 1 bar. Hold 30–60 min at 450–500 °C, then cool to 300 °C at 2–3 °C min−1 before unloading. Aim to approach optimal oxygenation without inducing excessive twin boundary oxygen ordering that would disrupt strain tuning.

Step10: Ex-situ oxygenation tuning. For the oxygenation series, perform post-anneals at 400–500 °C in flowing O2 (1 bar) for 0.5–4 h on select coupons to fine-tune δ. Measure Tc by four-probe resistivity and adjust anneal parameters to maximize Tc while preserving microstrain.

Step11: Thickness and rate verification. Measure film thickness at multiple positions along and across the tape using stylus profilometry on masked steps or cross-sectional SEM. Confirm average growth rate per pass and per turn; verify thickness uniformity (±10%) across 1–2 m segments.

Step12: Structural phase identification and lattice parameter determination. Perform XRD θ–2θ scans to confirm epitaxial c-axis EuBCO and presence of BSHO secondary phase with out-of-plane alignment. Extract the EuBCO c-lattice parameter from (00l) peak positions with substrate peak referencing and account for refraction corrections. Target c ≈ 11.744 Å; iterate oxygenation if needed.

Step13: Texture characterization. Measure rocking curves (ω) for EuBCO (00l) to quantify out-of-plane texture; perform φ scans (e.g., EuBCO {103}) to quantify in-plane texture. Aim for Δω ≈ 1.5° and Δφ ≈ 2.6°. For long-length tapes, map Δω and Δφ every 0.5 m to assess uniformity.

Step14: Williamson–Hall microstrain analysis. Collect high-resolution XRD of multiple EuBCO reflections spanning different l and h/k indices. Perform Williamson–Hall plots to separate size and strain broadening; compute microstrain ε and target ε ≈ 0.29%. Cross-validate with peak asymmetry and instrumental broadening standards.

Step15: TEM/STEM microstructure analysis. Prepare cross-section and plan-view lamellae by focused ion beam (low-kV final polish to reduce damage). Acquire HAADF-STEM at 200–300 kV to visualize BSHO columns; quantify:
- Column diameter distribution (mean target ~5 nm).
- Areal density by plan-view counting over ≥10 μm2 (target ~2200 μm−2).
- Column alignment and splay angle distribution relative to c-axis (target <12°).
- Continuity through thickness and interruptions (stripe-like EuBCO regions).
- Interfacial defect structure: identify semi-coherent BSHO/EuBCO interfaces and count misfit dislocations per a/b-axis.
Use geometric phase analysis (GPA) to map local strain fields around columns.

Step16: STEM-EDS/EELS composition profiling. Perform line scans and maps across multiple columns to determine Sn:Hf distribution within BSHO and at the BSHO/EuBCO interface. Confirm formation of solid solution BaSnxHf1−xO3 and assess any Sn- or Hf-rich shells/cores. Use EELS (O-K, Cu-L2,3) to probe oxygen deficiency near interfaces as a proxy for vacancy formation. Correlate with GPA strain maps.

Step17: Depth profiling of dopants. Use time-of-flight SIMS on select coupons to study Sn and Hf depth distribution and uniformity along thickness. Confirm absence of surface segregation or substrate-side enrichment that could indicate mobility imbalance at ultra-high rate.

Step18: Electrical patterning for transport measurements. Define bridges (e.g., 50–100 μm width, 0.5–2 mm length) by photolithography and Ar ion milling or by precision laser scribing. Deposit contact pads (Au, 100–200 nm with Ti or Cr adhesion) and anneal at 200 °C for 10 min to reduce contact resistance. Attach four-probe contacts with silver epoxy; cure appropriately.

Step19: Superconducting transition and self-field Jc. Measure R(T) to determine Tc onset and zero resistance. At 77 K, measure self-field Jc using a 1 μV cm−1 criterion; record E–J curves to confirm n-values ≥ 20. Use multiple bridges along the tape to assess homogeneity.

Step20: High-field angular transport measurements. In a 18–25 T superconducting or cryogen-free magnet with a rotatable sample stage:
- Measure Jc(B, T, θ) from 4.2 K to 77 K, B up to 24–25 T, θ spanning −90° to +90° with ≤2° step near c-axis to resolve correlated pinning peaks.
- Use a 1 μV cm−1 criterion. Measure both perpendicular (B ⟂ tape plane, ~c-axis) and parallel orientations.
- Determine pinning force Fp(B, T) = Jc μ0 H and assess saturation behavior up to maximum field.
- Extract matching field Bφ from c-axis peak features and/or from the measured nanocolumn density (Bφ ≈ nΦ0) for comparison.
- Quantify splay-induced broadening and Jc(θ) anisotropy.

Step21: Pinning analysis and scaling. Fit Fp(b) with Dew-Hughes/Kramer models to deconvolute correlated (nanocolumn) versus random (dislocation/oxygen vacancy) contributions; analyze temperature dependence to separate core- and δTc-type pinning. Apply anisotropic scaling (Blatter) to assess mass anisotropy versus correlated pinning effects.

Step22: Control comparisons to validate synergy. Repeat Steps18–21 on:
- BSO-only and BHO-only APC films at 8 mol% total.
- Co-doped films with varied BSO:BHO ratios.
Compare Jc(B, T, θ), Fp,max, and Bφ to establish that co-doping enhances nucleation density (via Sn) and limits radial growth (via Hf), yielding smaller, denser columns and additional random pinning.

Step23: Process refinement loop. Using TEM/XRD/transport feedback:
- If columns are >5 nm or density <2000 μm−2, reduce substrate temperature by 10–20 °C and/or increase growth rate to curtail lateral diffusion; adjust BHO fraction upward slightly (e.g., 3.5→4.0 mol%) to further limit radial growth while maintaining total at 8 mol%.
- If columns are discontinuous with excessive splay, increase pO2 modestly (e.g., +50 mTorr) and/or reduce web speed for better adatom mobility.
- If microstrain <0.25% or macrocracks appear, tweak oxygenation (slightly lower post-anneal temperature/time) and adjust BSO:BHO to tune lattice mismatch.

Step24: Long-length uniformity and reliability tests. On 5–20 m tape segments:
- Map Jc at 77 K self-field and at 50 K, 3 T (B ⟂) every 0.5 m using non-destructive transport or scanning Hall probe magnetometry with local transport verification.
- Perform bending strain tests (±0.4% tensile/compressive) and 50 thermal cycles (300↔50 K) on short coupons; remeasure Jc(B, T, θ) to assess retention and microstructure stability.

Step25: Documentation and data correlation. Compile correlations between: (a) column diameter/density/splay and Bφ, Fp,max; (b) interface dislocation density/oxygen vacancy signatures and high-field Jc slopes; (c) Δφ/Δω and Jc anisotropy. Define the processing window that reproducibly yields ≈5 nm, ≈2200 μm−2 BSHO columns, c ≈ 11.744 Å, Δφ ≈ 2.6°, Δω ≈ 1.5°, microstrain ≈ 0.29%, and optimized in-field transport performance suitable for ≥5 T at 50 K or ≥20 T at 20 K applications.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1: Target preparation  
- A single high-density ceramic target is prepared with the nominal composition: EuBCO + 3.5 mol % BHO + 4.5 mol % BSO (total dopant 8 mol %).  
- Target phase purity is checked by laboratory X-ray diffraction (θ–2θ scan shown in fig. S1).

Step 2: Substrate provision  
- Commercial buffered metallic tapes are used: Hastelloy/Al₂O₃/Y₂O₃/IBAD-MgO/LaMnO₃/CeO₂.  
- 12-mm-wide tapes are loaded on the reel-to-reel supply spool of the PLD system.

Step 3: Reel-to-reel multi-plume & multi-turn PLD growth  
- Deposition is performed in a custom reel-to-reel PLD chamber equipped with a Coherent LEAP-300 excimer laser.  
- Table 1 lists fixed parameters:  
  – Substrate temperature 880–920 °C  
  – Oxygen pressure 400–600 mTorr  
  – Laser energy 500–700 mJ per pulse  
  – Peak growth rate >100 nm s⁻¹  
  – Tape travelling speed 50–60 m h⁻¹  
- The final superconducting layer thickness is 1 µm.

Step 4: Post-deposition silver contacting  
- Without breaking vacuum, a 2 µm Ag layer is deposited on the fresh EuBCO surface (PLD or sputter method not specified).

Step 5: Oxygenation  
- The Ag-coated tape is oxygenated for 3 h at 350–400 °C in flowing O₂ atmosphere, then furnace-cooled.

Step 6: Structural / textural characterisation  
- θ–2θ scans (10–60°) and rocking curves on EuBCO (005) are recorded with a Bruker D8 Advance four-circle X-ray diffractometer (2-D detector) to verify c-axis orientation and out-of-plane texture.  
- φ-scans on EuBCO (103) (ω₀ = 16.4°, χ = 45.6°, φ 0–360°) quantify in-plane texture.  
- Lattice parameter and micro-strain are extracted by Nelson–Riley and Williamson–Hall methods, respectively.

Step 7: Microstructure & chemistry analysis  
- Cross-sectional and plan-view TEM specimens are prepared by Ga-ion milling in a TESCAN GAIA3 dual-beam FIB (1–40 kV).  
- Imaging and compositional mapping are carried out in a ThermoFisher Talos F200X and a Spectra 300 probe-corrected TEM (200 kV, cold FEG) equipped with Super-X EDS.  
- Nanocolumn diameter, length, splay angle and areal density are measured from STEM images.  
- EDS line-scans across enlarged (bevel-cut) columns give local Hf:Sn ratio.

Step 8: Transport critical-current measurements  
- 4-mm-wide short samples are cut from the tape.  
- A 40 µm × 1 mm micro-bridge is laser-etched through the Ag and EuBCO layers.  
- Four-probe I–V curves are recorded:  
  – Self-field Jc at 77 K in a liquid-N₂ bath (1 µV cm⁻¹ criterion).  
  – In-field Jc(θ) and Jc(B) at 50 K, 20 K and 4.2 K using:  
    • 18 T superconducting magnet (for ≤18 T)  
    • 25 T cryogen-free superconducting magnet (for ≤24 T)  
  – Angular range θ = −45° to 135° (θ = 0° means H‖c-axis).  
- Pinning force density Fp = Jc × B is calculated; the data are fitted with a cooperative random-plus-correlated pinning model (eqs 1–3) to separate correlated and random contributions.

[Experimental Design Details]
- Dopant choice: 3.5 mol % BHO + 4.5 mol % BSO (total 8 mol %) chosen to balance nucleation density (Sn) and growth restriction (Hf).  
- Growth rate: >100 nm s⁻¹ (one to two orders faster than conventional PLD).  
- Film thickness targeted at 1 µm; Ag over-layer 2 µm.  
- Oxygenation conditions: 3 h, 350–400 °C, O₂ atmosphere (cooling profile not specified).  
- Transport bridge geometry: 40 µm wide, 1 mm long, defined by laser etching (edge quality not detailed).  
- Electric-field criterion for Jc: 1 µV cm⁻¹.  
- Field orientation: θ = 0° corresponds to H perpendicular to the tape plane (H‖c-axis).

Experiment: Step1: Define objectives and variables. Goal: maximize in-field Jc at 20 K (8–10 T) for epitaxial (Y0.8RE'0.2−xRE''x)Ba2Cu3O7−y thin films on SrTiO3, with controlled incidental (Y,RE',RE'')2O3 nanoparticles ≤14 nm, using fixed growth temperature (790 °C), liquid-assisted growth (+L, via BaCu2O2) and layer-by-layer deposition (+LLD). Variables: RE mixing (Y, Gd, Yb, Dy, Ho, Sm, Nd), ion-size variance σr2, BaCu2O2 fraction (0–35 mol%), deposition protocol (SSD, +L, +L+LLD), thickness (200–400 nm), oxygenation schedule. Controls: pure YBCO films under SSD and +L+LLD.

Step2: Calculate RE ionic-size statistics. Use Shannon 3+ radii (8-fold coordination) to compute average radius ravg and variance σr2 for each composition. Select the primary composition (Y0.8Gd0.1Yb0.1) to match ravg ≈ r(Y3+) and moderate σr2 (~2–3×10−4). Prepare comparison sets with increased σr2 (e.g., partial substitution with Nd, Sm, Dy, Ho) and decreased σr2 (single-RE substitution) while maintaining ravg ≈ r(Y3+).

Step3: Prepare PLD ceramic targets. a) YREBCO targets: weigh high-purity (>99.99%) Y2O3, RE'2O3, RE''2O3, BaCO3, CuO to achieve (Y0.8RE'0.2−xRE''x)Ba2Cu3O7−δ stoichiometry. Ball-mill with isopropanol 24 h, dry, calcine 900–920 °C in flowing O2 for 12 h with intermediate grindings, then press and sinter 930–950 °C in O2 for 24 h. Polish face to reduce particulates. b) Pure YBCO target (for control) prepared similarly. c) BaCu2O2 target: mix BaCO3 and CuO in 1:1 molar ratio, calcine 800–830 °C in flowing O2 with repeated grindings until single-phase BaCu2O2 is confirmed by XRD; press and sinter at 820–850 °C; store and handle in dry conditions. Prepare multiple RE-mixed targets covering the composition series.

Step4: Calibrate ablation rates. In the PLD chamber, at room temperature, ablate each target separately onto witness substrates (e.g., LaAlO3 or Si with native oxide) at representative fluence. Determine deposition rate per pulse by profilometry or quartz crystal microbalance. Repeat at 790 °C/200–300 mTorr O2 to account for temperature-dependent sticking. Use these rates to translate the desired BaCu2O2 mol% into pulse fractions for co-ablation.

Step5: Substrate preparation (SrTiO3, (001), single-side polished). Ultrasonically clean in acetone/IPA, dry N2. Achieve TiO2 termination and atomically flat terraces: etch in buffered HF (NH4F:HF) or hot deionized water depending on protocol, rinse, then anneal in air at 950–1000 °C for 1–2 h. Verify step-terrace morphology by AFM (terrace widths consistent with miscut; rms roughness ≤0.2 nm).

Step6: PLD system setup. Use a KrF excimer laser (248 nm). Set fluence 1.5–2.0 J cm−2; spot size ~2–4 mm2; target rotation. Target–substrate distance 45–55 mm. Substrate heater calibrated to 790 °C (pyrometer). Chamber base pressure ≤1×10−6 Torr. Oxygen partial pressure during growth 200–300 mTorr (optimize within this window). Optional: enable in-situ RHEED for growth-mode monitoring.

Step7: Define film thickness and patterning plan. Target thickness 300 nm for primary comparisons (also prepare 200 and 400 nm to check thickness dependence). Plan lithographic patterning of 25 µm-wide bridges for four-probe transport. Prepare sacrificial samples for cross-sectional TEM.

Step8: Deposition protocol A (SSD, solid-state PLD). a) Heat substrate to 790 °C, stabilize 10–15 min at 250 mTorr O2. b) Ablate YREBCO (or YBCO control) at 5–10 Hz to deposit 300 nm (track pulses via prior calibration). c) Cool to 500 °C at 10 °C/min in 300 Torr O2 (backfill), dwell 30 min for oxygen uptake, then cool to room temperature at 5 °C/min. d) Optionally, post-anneal in pure O2 at 400–450 °C for 1 h to optimize oxygenation.

Step9: Deposition protocol B (+L, liquid-assisted PLD with BaCu2O2). a) Heat to 790 °C, 250 mTorr O2. b) Co-ablation strategy: implement pulse sequence X:Y between YREBCO and BaCu2O2 such that BaCu2O2 contributes 26 mol% of total arrived cations (use Step4 calibration). Example: 3 pulses YREBCO : 1 pulse BaCu2O2 repeated (adjust if rates differ). Alternatively, deposit ultra-thin BaCu2O2 sublayers (≤0.5 nm) every 2–3 nm of YREBCO. c) Maintain laser repetition 10–20 Hz effective. d) Finish with a brief YREBCO-only cap (5–10 nm) to avoid Ba–Cu–O-rich surface. e) Oxygenation as in Step8c–d.

Step10: Deposition protocol C (+L+LLD, liquid-assisted layer-by-layer). a) Same as Step9 but implement LLD cycles: high-frequency burst (e.g., 50 Hz) for N pulses (equivalent to ~1–2 unit cells), then pause 5–10 s for surface relaxation; during each burst follow co-ablation ratio achieving 26 mol% BaCu2O2; repeat until 300 nm. b) Monitor RHEED intensity oscillations if available to maintain near-layer-by-layer growth; adjust pause duration to recover specular intensity. c) Oxygenation as in Step8c–d.

Step11: Prevent particulates and ensure interface quality. Pre-ablate each target for 2–5 min before growth. Maintain target surface smoothness by periodic polishing. Check plume stability and minimize splashing by optimizing fluence and spot focus. Use off-axis geometry if particulate density is high.

Step12: Composition verification. Use X-ray fluorescence (XRF) or Rutherford backscattering spectrometry (RBS) to confirm cation ratios (Y:RE:Ba:Cu) in the films. For thin-film sensitivity to RE distribution, complement with STEM-EDX line scans and maps. Confirm that the average A-site (Y+RE) stoichiometry is unity and that ravg ≈ r(Y3+) in the films.

Step13: Structural characterization by XRD. a) θ–2θ scans (Cu Kα) to confirm c-axis oriented YBCO phase (00l peaks) and absence/minimization of secondary phases at detectable levels. b) Rocking curves (ω) of YBCO (005) and (007); target FWHM ≤0.2–0.25° for +L+LLD. c) In-plane φ-scans of (103) to assess in-plane texture (fourfold symmetry, FWHMφ ≤0.5–0.8°). d) Reciprocal space maps around (103)/(013) to assess lattice parameters, strain state, and mosaic spread. e) X-ray reflectivity (XRR) for thickness and roughness.

Step14: Surface morphology by AFM. Scan 2×2 µm and 5×5 µm areas. Record rms roughness; look for step-flow terraces in +LLD films. Correlate roughness with rocking curve widths.

Step15: Microstructure and nanoparticle analysis by STEM. Prepare cross-sectional lamellae by FIB with low-kV final polish. Acquire HAADF-STEM to visualize (Y,RE)2O3 nanoparticles and their distribution; measure size distribution and areal number density; target mean diameter ≤14 nm with relatively uniform spacing. Perform EDX/EELS to identify nanoparticle composition and YREBCO/RE2O3 interface coherence. Quantify dislocation density and any stacking faults. Compare SSD vs +L vs +L+LLD.

Step16: Raman spectroscopy. Collect spectra (e.g., 514 nm excitation) to assess oxygen ordering (B1g modes), chain vibrations, and detect strain signatures. Compare peak positions/widths across protocols to evaluate lattice healing by BaCu2O2.

Step17: Electrical contact patterning for transport. a) Deposit 50–100 nm Au pads through a shadow mask or by lithography (with gentle Ar ion clean prior to Au sputter/evaporation). b) Pattern 25 µm-wide bridges with 100–200 µm voltage tap spacing by photolithography and Ar ion milling (or wet etch in dilute H3PO4 for YBCO with careful endpoint). Protect film during processing to preserve oxygenation; re-oxygenate at 350–400 °C in O2 for 30–60 min if needed.

Step18: Superconducting transition and normal-state characterization. Measure resistivity ρ(T) from 300 K to 10 K; determine Tc onset and zero resistance (seek Tc ≥ 90 K for optimally oxygenated films). Check residual resistivity and RRR as proxies for disorder.

Step19: Critical current density measurements. a) Mount patterned samples in a cryostat with 20 K capability and 0–10 T superconducting magnet. b) Four-probe transport Jc with 0.2 µV cm−1 criterion; fields applied parallel to c-axis (H||c). c) Measure Jc(H) at 20 K from 0 to 10 T; repeat at 30 K and 77 K for benchmarking. d) Angle-dependent Jc(θ) at 20 K, 3 T and 8 T to identify pinning anisotropy (θ=0° is H||c). e) Compute engineering Fp(B)=µ0 Jc B and perform Dew-Hughes scaling to infer dominant pinning (point vs surface, normal core vs δl/δTc type).

Step20: Comparative matrix and replication. For each composition and protocol (SSD, +L, +L+LLD), prepare at least three nominally identical films to establish reproducibility. Include pure YBCO controls under SSD and +L+LLD. Construct a matrix varying σr2 (e.g., Y0.8Gd0.2, Y0.8Gd0.1Yb0.1, Y0.8Gd0.05Yb0.05Nd0.1, etc.) at fixed 790 °C and fixed BaCu2O2 fraction (0% and 26%). Optionally, vary BaCu2O2 fraction (0, 10, 26, 35 mol%) at fixed composition to confirm the optimum.

Step21: Data analysis and optimization. a) Correlate Jc(20 K, 8 T) with σr2, nanoparticle size/density, and structural metrics (Δω, Δ2θ, φ-FWHM, AFM roughness). b) Identify the σr2 range where nanoparticle pinning outweighs atomic-scale disorder. c) Evaluate the effect of +L on rocking-curve widths and nanoparticle/YREBCO interface quality from TEM/EELS. d) Quantify the incremental benefit of +LLD on texture and Jc. e) Confirm that compositions with ravg≈r(Y3+) exhibit minimal macroscopic strain (from RSM) and superior Jc. f) Benchmark the optimized +L+LLD Y0.8Gd0.1Yb0.1 film against pure YBCO.

Step22: Troubleshooting and process adjustments. a) If rocking-curve FWHM >0.25° in +L+LLD, reduce deposition rate per cycle, increase relaxation pause, or slightly increase pO2 (up to 300–400 mTorr) to enhance adatom mobility; verify target surface condition. b) If nanoparticle size exceeds 14 nm, decrease substrate temperature by 10–20 °C or reduce BaCu2O2 fraction to limit coarsening; increase LLD pause to prevent coalescence. c) If Tc is suppressed, adjust oxygenation (higher O2 pressure/longer dwell at 400–500 °C), verify cation stoichiometry, and reduce σr2. d) If particulates degrade surface, lower fluence, adjust spot imaging, or adopt off-axis deposition. e) If interfacial misfit increases, ensure STO termination quality and consider a thin buffer (e.g., LaMnO3) for subsequent coated-conductor translation.

Step23: Validation of liquid-assisted healing. Use STEM to compare dislocation density and strain fields around nanoparticles in SSD vs +L vs +L+LLD. Assess coherence of YREBCO/RE2O3 interfaces (lattice fringes continuity) and quantify strain mapping via geometric phase analysis. Expect +L to reduce extended defects and maintain coherent interfaces, enabling pinning benefits to dominate.

Step24: Longitudinal stability and oxygen retention. Store a subset of films at room temperature and 100 °C in dry air for 1–2 weeks; remeasure Tc and Jc to ensure BaCu2O2-assisted growth does not compromise oxygen stability. Optionally cap with ~10 nm Au to reduce surface oxygen loss.

Step25: Extension to coated-conductor relevant substrates (optional follow-up). Transfer the optimized +L+LLD recipe to IBAD-MgO/LMO-buffered Hastelloy templates at 790 °C (adjust to substrate limitations), maintaining 26 mol% BaCu2O2 and Y0.8Gd0.1Yb0.1 composition. Repeat Steps13–21 to assess scalability for magnet applications at 20 K.

Step26: Documentation and reporting. Record all deposition parameters (temperatures, pO2, fluence, repetition rates, pulse sequences, relaxation times), target history, substrate preparation details, and measurement configurations for each sample. Archive raw XRD, AFM, STEM, Raman, and transport data with metadata to enable reproducibility and cross-lab comparison.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1: Target synthesis  
- Commercial 99 % purity RE₂O₃ (RE = Yb, Er, Ho, Y, Dy, Gd, Eu, Sm, Nd), BaCO₃ and CuO powders are weighed and mixed to the cation ratio 1 RE : 2 Ba : 3 Cu.  
- 5 wt % stearic acid is added as lubricant, the powder is ground, pressed into a green compact and heated in flowing O₂ at 900 °C for 12–24 h.  
- The grind/press/sinter cycle is repeated ≥ 2 times to ensure full reaction and densification.  
- Two target variants are prepared for each composition:  
  (i) stoichiometric 1:2:3 (labelled “SSD” or “Y,RE”)  
  (ii) off-stoichiometric (Y,RE′,RE″)Ba₁.₇Cu₂.₇O₇₋x containing 26 mol % extra liquid (assumed BaCu₂O₂) (labelled “Y,RE + L”).  

Step 2: Substrate preparation  
- Single-crystal SrTiO₃ (STO) substrates are used as-received; no further surface treatment details are given.

Step 3: Film deposition  
- PLD is carried out with a Lambda Physik KrF excimer laser (λ = 248 nm, fluence ≈ 2 J cm⁻², target–substrate distance 55 mm, target rotating).  
- Base growth conditions: substrate temperature 790 °C, pO₂ = 0.2 mTorr.  
- Three processing routes are explored:  
  (1) Standard solid-state deposition (SSD) at 5 Hz → growth rate 0.020 µm min⁻¹ (0.33 nm s⁻¹).  
  (2) Liquid-assisted deposition (Y,RE + L) at 5 Hz → same rate as (1).  
  (3) Layer-by-layer deposition (Y,RE + L + LLD) at 50 Hz with relaxation cycles; growth temperature raised to 820 °C to reduce disorder; growth rate 0.035 µm min⁻¹ (0.58 nm s⁻¹).  
- All films receive the same post-anneal: 550 °C, 500 Torr O₂, 1 h.  

Step 4: Patterning for transport  
- Films are patterned by standard photolithography into 25 µm-wide, 2–5 mm-long bridges.  
- Silver contact pads are deposited for four-point measurements.

Step 5: Structural characterisation  
- X-ray diffraction (Philips PW3020, Cu Kα, Bragg–Brentano geometry): θ–2θ scans and rocking-curve (ω) scans of the REBCO (005) reflection.

Step 1: Buffer-layer deposition  
- Substrate: (001) LaAlO₃ single-crystal substrates.  
- Target composition: SrTiO₃ (STO) + x CeO₂ with x = 0 %, 30 %, 50 % (nominal weight fractions; equivalent to 0, 22.2, 39.9 vol % CeO₂).  
- Method: Pulsed-laser deposition (PLD) using a KrF excimer laser (λ = 243 nm).

- Target: stoichiometric YBa₂Cu₃O₇.  
- Method: same PLD system, 6000 pulses, 10 Hz, 200 mTorr O₂, substrate temperature identical to that used for the underlying buffer layer (800 °C or 850 °C).  
- Resulting film thickness: not explicitly stated in the paper.  

Step 3: Device patterning for transport measurements  
- Au electrodes deposited by sputtering.  
- Conventional photolithography and H₃PO₄ wet etching used to define a 1 mm × 100 µm bridge.  

Step 4: Critical-current measurement  
- Instrument: Quantum Design Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS).  
- Criterion: 10 µV cm⁻¹.  
- Magnetic field: applied perpendicular to the film plane.  
- Temperatures: 65 K and 77 K.  

Step 5: Microstructural characterisation  
- Sample preparation: cross-sectional and plan-view TEM/STEM foils cut with a Thermo Scientific Scios 2 DualBeam FIB (Ga ions: 30 kV coarse milling → 2 kV final polish).  
- Instruments:  
  – JEOL JEM-3000F and JEM-F200 operated at 200 kV for bright-field (BF) and high-resolution TEM.  
  – JEM-F200 equipped with EDX for elemental mapping (Sr-L, Ti-K, Ce-L, Y-L, Ba-L, Cu-K lines).  
- Imaging conditions: two-beam BF conditions with g = [001] and g = [010] to establish Burgers vector of linear defects.  

[Experimental Design Details]
- Buffer-layer architecture: intentionally phase-separated into vertically aligned CeO₂ “nanowalls” within an STO matrix (period ≈ 20 nm) confirmed by cross-sectional and plan-view STEM-EDX.  
- Interface engineering: the rough, nanoparticle-decorated YBCO/buffer interface (BaCeO₃ and Y₂O₃ precipitates) serves as nucleation sites for threading dislocations.  
- Dislocation density control: varied by CeO₂ content (30 % vs 50 %) and deposition temperature (800 °C vs 850 °C).  Highest density achieved: ≈ 150 µm⁻².  
- Matching field estimate: nw₀ ≈ 0.3 T for the highest dislocation density (n = 150 µm⁻², w₀ = 2.07 × 10⁻¹⁵ T m²).

Experiment: Step1: Define experimental objectives and metrics: quantify the effect of Dy 4f magnetism on intergranular Josephson coupling by comparing Tc2J, Tc1g, Tc2J–Tc1g width, and E–J characteristics in granular YBa2Cu3O7−δ (Y-123) and DyBa2Cu3O7−δ (Dy-123) processed identically; ensure microstructure, oxygen content, density, and contact protocol are held constant.

Step2: Prepare starting powders: high-purity Y2O3 or Dy2O3 (≥99.99%), BaCO3 (≥99.99%), and CuO (≥99.99%). Dry at 200 °C for 2 h to remove adsorbed moisture and CO2. Weigh stoichiometric ratios for ReBa2Cu3O7−δ.

Step3: First calcination and mixing: wet-mix powders in isopropanol with zirconia media for 12 h, dry, then calcine in flowing oxygen or air at 900 °C for 12 h (heating/cooling 3 °C/min). Grind thoroughly and re-calcine once more at 920 °C for 12 h to complete BaCO3 decomposition and promote phase formation.

Step4: Press green bodies: sieve powders (≤75 µm), add 1–2 wt% PVA binder, press pellets of identical dimensions (e.g., 12 mm diameter, 2 mm thickness) using identical uniaxial pressing load (as specified, 650 kg mm⁻² equivalent load conditions) to achieve matched green densities (target 60–65% theoretical). Record dimension and mass.

Step5: Sintering: place pellets on sacrificial powder of the same composition to minimize Ba/Cu loss; sinter both compositions in the same furnace run at 950 °C for 24 h in flowing oxygen or air. Use identical heating/cooling rates (5 °C/min). Ensure both batches share the same thermal profile and position in the furnace to minimize temperature gradients.

Step6: Oxygenation anneal and stress control: anneal in flowing oxygen at 500 °C for 24 h, then slow cool at 5 °C/min to room temperature. Record the full thermal history. This sets oxygen ordering and relieves thermal stress identically for both compositions.

Step7: Density matching: measure bulk density by geometric method and Archimedes. If densities differ by >2%, adjust pressing or sintering and remake until densities match within ±2%, to keep demagnetization and percolation paths comparable.

Step8: Contact deposition (identical protocol): after oxygenation, rf-sputter 200–300 nm silver pads through a mask to define a standard four-probe geometry (contact spacing and width identical across samples). Attach 25 µm Ag wires with silver epoxy cured at ≤120 °C for 30 min in flowing oxygen. Verify contact resistance at 100 K is ≪1% of sample resistance above Tc.

Step9: Phase purity and lattice parameters: perform powder X-ray diffraction (Cu Kα, 2θ = 15–75°, step 0.01°). Rietveld refine to confirm orthorhombic Pmmm, quantify secondary phases (<3% threshold). Extract a, b, c, and orthorhombicity Δ; ensure both samples show the expected orthorhombic phase.

Step10: Oxygen content verification: measure δ by iodometric titration on fragments from each pellet (triplicates) or by thermogravimetric reduction in H2 to extract oxygen content. Accept only pairs where δ matches within ±0.01; otherwise repeat oxygenation.

Step11: Microstructure matching: SEM on polished and thermally etched surfaces to measure grain size distribution (≥500 grains per sample). Target mean grain size ~1 µm with standard deviation matched within ±10% between Y-123 and Dy-123. Assess porosity and second phases at grain boundaries. Optional FIB cross-sections to estimate boundary thickness.

Step12: Texture assessment: XRD texture (pole figures) or EBSD if feasible to confirm random grain orientation and absence of macroscopic texture. Ensure both compositions exhibit similar texture statistics.

Step13: Magnetic background characterization: measure M(T) for both samples using SQUID or VSM from 300 K to 10 K in a small field (e.g., 100 Oe), zero-field-cooled (ZFC) and field-cooled (FC). Fit the normal-state (T > 100 K) susceptibility to extract the Curie-Weiss contribution from Dy in Dy-123; confirm Y-123 is magnetically neutral aside from weak Pauli/Van Vleck terms.

Step14: AC susceptibility to resolve Tc1g vs intergranular coupling: measure χ′(T), χ″(T) at Hac = 1–5 Oe, f = 10–1000 Hz, ZFC. Identify high-T diamagnetic onset (Tc1g, intragrain) and low-T intergranular coupling onset; verify Tc1g is similar in both compositions (within ~1 K if δ matched) and that differences in intergranular onset correlate with Dy magnetism.

Step15: Transport setup and calibration: mount pellets in a cryostat with stable temperature control (±5 mK). Use the same four-probe geometry and current density j = 2 A cm⁻² (e.g., 10 mA for the chosen cross-section). Align a pair of Nd2Fe14B magnets to apply a transverse field perpendicular to the current. Calibrate field at the sample position with a Hall probe at room temperature and at 77 K; map uniformity over sample area (±1%). Verify demagnetization factors are comparable via identical geometry.

Step16: Field-cooled resistivity vs temperature: for each field Hext = 0, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 1500, 1900 Oe, cool the sample from 120 K to 60 K in the set field at a controlled rate of 0.002–0.004 K s⁻¹ (FC protocol). Record ρ(T) continuously at j = 2 A cm⁻². Repeat three cycles to assess repeatability and absence of training effects. Perform the same sequence on Y-123 and Dy-123.

Step17: Tc extraction criteria: define Tc1g from AC susceptibility high-T onset (Step14). Define Tc2J as the temperature at which finite resistivity first appears upon warming in FC measurement at the given H (onset criterion ρ > 1 nΩ·cm or above noise floor), corroborated by a feature in dρ/dT. Determine the zero-resistance temperature T0 for each field. Compute Tc2J–Tc1g and T0–Tc2J widths with uncertainties.

Step18: Orientation check (isotropy control): repeat ρ(T) at Hext = 250 Oe and 1000 Oe with the sample rotated by 90° around the current axis (field still transverse) to test for anisotropy arising from texture. Expect no systematic orientation dependence for randomly oriented ceramics; confirm identical behavior within error.

Step19: I–V characterization near 77 K: at fixed T = 77 K and selected fields (0, 250, 500, 1000, 1500, 1900 Oe), measure V–I curves from subcritical to dissipative regime. Fit E–J to power law E ∝ J^n to extract n-values and critical current density Jc (criterion E = 1 µV cm⁻¹). Compare Dy-123 vs Y-123; expect lower Jc and n for Dy-123 at the same field if internal magnetism enhances weak-link dissipation.

Step20: Resistivity vs field at fixed temperature: at T = 80, 77, 72 K, ramp Hext from 0 to 1900 Oe in steps of 50–100 Oe in FC mode, recording ρ(H). Identify onset field for dissipation and quantify sensitivity to Dy 4f magnetism.

Step21: Magneto-optical imaging (optional but recommended): use a Bi-doped iron-garnet indicator film on polished pellet surfaces at 77–85 K to visualize flux penetration under 100–1000 Oe. Compare flux entry along grain boundaries in Y-123 and Dy-123 to qualitatively assess enhanced weak-link vortex nucleation with Dy.

Step22: Series with partial Dy substitution (tuning study): prepare Y1−xDyxBa2Cu3O7−δ ceramics for x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 using the identical processing and characterization pipeline. Repeat Steps9–20 to map Tc2J(x), Tc1g(x), and Tc2J–Tc1g(x) under fixed fields (e.g., 250 and 1000 Oe), establishing a trend between Dy content and intergranular suppression.

Step23: Contact and self-field controls: confirm that contact resistance and self-field from the transport current are negligible contributors by repeating ρ(T) at j = 1 and 3 A cm⁻² at H = 250 Oe; verify Tc2J shifts within measurement uncertainty. Ensure contact protocol (thickness, curing) is identical across all samples.

Step24: Data analysis and uncertainty: compute mean and standard deviation for Tc1g, Tc2J, Tc2J–Tc1g, T0, Jc, and n across at least three pellets per composition. Propagate uncertainties from temperature calibration, field calibration, and contact spacing. Plot Tc2J vs H and Tc2J–Tc1g vs H for Y-123 and Dy-123 and for Y1−xDyx series.

Step25: Correlation with magnetic background: correlate Dy-induced paramagnetic susceptibility (Step13) with shifts in Tc2J and broadening Tc2J–Tc1g to establish the link between 4f magnetism and weak-link dissipation. Verify that Tc1g remains nearly unchanged with Dy at matched δ, confirming the intergranular origin of differences.

Step26: Application-relevant metrics at 77 K: extract Jc(77 K, H = 0–1900 Oe) and n-values for both compositions; determine the maximum field at which Y-123 maintains T0 ≥ 77 K at H = 250–1900 Oe versus Dy-123. Summarize implications for 77 K device operation.

Step27: Reproducibility and batch effects: repeat the full synthesis and measurement on an independent batch to confirm the robustness of the observed differences. If batch-to-batch variations exceed 5%, tighten processing controls (powder mixing time, sintering atmosphere monitoring, oxygen flow).

Step28: Documentation and data integrity: archive raw XRD, SEM, titration, magnetometry, ac susceptibility, transport, and imaging data with metadata on processing parameters. Maintain traceable links between pellets and measurement datasets.

Step29: Safety and quality controls: handle rare-earth oxides and fine CuO powders in a fume hood with PPE; ensure oxygen anneals are performed with proper venting; manage strong permanent magnets with non-magnetic tools and guards; verify electrical safety on cryostat wiring.

Step30: Decision criteria: accept the hypothesis if, under matched δ, microstructure, and contacts, Dy-123 shows (i) a statistically significant lower Tc2J (e.g., ≳5 K at 250 Oe) than Y-123, (ii) a wider Tc2J–Tc1g window across fields, and (iii) reduced Jc and n at 77 K under the same H, while Tc1g remains within ≈1 K across compositions. Otherwise, revisit oxygen stoichiometry, microstructure, and measurement protocol for confounding factors.

- Dy-123 bars given a final anneal at 500 °C in “oxidizing environment” followed by slow furnace cool; Y-123 final anneal conditions not stated.

Step 4: Sample certification  
- Crush part of each bar into powder.  
- X-ray diffraction (DRON UM-1, Bragg–Brentano, Cu Kα, 2θ = 15–75°, step 0.1°; triplet 006/200/020 resolved with Gaussian fit, Δ2θ ≈0.01°) to confirm single-phase orthorhombic Pmmm and to extract lattice parameters (accuracy 10⁻⁴ Å).  
- Resistive Tc (and magnetic Tc, method not detailed) taken from ρ(T) at H = 0; Tc defined as temperature of maximum dρ/dT. Recorded Tc = 92.6 ± 0.01 K (Y-123) and 90.5 ± 0.01 K (Dy-123).

Step 5: Transport measurement protocol  
- Mount bar in home-built cryostat.  
- Cool in field (FC) using pairs of Nd₂Fe₁₄B permanent magnets; field values Hext = 0, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 1400, 1900 Oe applied perpendicular to the long axis.  
- Maintain constant dc transport current density j = 2 A cm⁻² (I = 10 mA).  
- Sweep temperature upward at 0.002–0.004 K s⁻¹ while recording four-probe resistance, giving ρ(T)Hext curves.  
- From each curve identify:  
  – Tc2J = Tρ=0 (onset of finite resistivity, weak-link transition)  
  – Tc1g = temperature of peak in dρ/dT (onset of Abrikosov-vortex penetration into grains)  
  – Tc (bulk transition, essentially field-independent).  

Step 6: Data reduction  
- Construct H–Tc phase diagrams for both sub-systems of each compound from the above characteristic temperatures.

- Sample geometry: ≈2 × 2 × 20 mm bars cut from pressed pellets.  
- Contact material: Ag, deposited by vacuum evaporation; contact resistance reduced by post-anneal (Dy-123).  
- Magnetic-field application: perpendicular to broad face; FC mode; field produced by permanent-magnet pairs (no superconducting coil mentioned).  
- Transport current: fixed at 10 mA (j = 2 A cm⁻²) for all runs; polarity reversal or pulsing not mentioned.  
- Temperature control: slow sweep 0.002–0.004 K s⁻¹ to ensure “maximum equilibrium”; absolute temperature error not quoted.  
- Criteria for critical temperatures explicitly defined in text; no mention of criterion for upper critical field Hc2.

- Electrical: Pulsed-current supply up to 1.5 kA, 4-probe measurement leads, shunt standards, low-noise preamps, DAQ ≥1 MS/s with simultaneous channels.
- Cryogenics: Pumped-LN₂ bath cryostat with ±0.05 K uniformity over 20 cm active length, 8–16-channel PT100 array and calibrator, heater control.
- Quench initiation: Small NdFeB magnet (surface field ~0.4–0.6 T) with positioning stage; optional 50–200 Ω thin-film heater with 10–50 ms pulses for cross-check.
- Safety: Cryogenic PPE, high-current interlocks, oxygen monitoring.

Step3: Baseline characterization of as-received tapes:
- Clean tape with isopropanol and N₂ dry. Cut 1 m and multiple 30 cm segments for baseline data.
- Measure Ic at 77 K, self-field using pulsed-current 4-probe (1 µV cm⁻¹ criterion) and extract n-value via E–I power-law fit; record uniformity along the 1 m length (≥3 positions).
- XRD: verify orthorhombic REBCO and biaxial texture; record Δω (rocking curve) and in-plane Δφ; target Δω <5°.
- Thickness and surface topography: measure Ag thickness and roughness; document for later comparison.

Step4: CFD design-of-experiments (DoE) for interface engineering:
- Pattern coverage: plan three variants (60%, 80%, 90% of width) with fixed edge low-Ri stripes to validate optimum; the primary target is 80% coverage (1.6 mm central CFD on each side of tape centerline if symmetric or a single 3.2 mm central CFD band leaving 0.4 mm low-Ri each edge).
- Interfacial resistance tuning: target nominal specific contact resistances of 100, 200, and 320 µΩ·cm² by varying amorphous barrier thickness (e.g., Al2O3 ALD 2, 3, 4.5 nm; calibrate separately).
- Controls: include (a) unmodified tapes; (b) full-width barrier (100%) to bound behavior; (c) barrier-free stripes on edges only to test lateral current transfer sensitivity.

Step5: Reel-to-reel patterning workflow (single-pass scalable line):
- Step5.1 (Surface preparation): If tape has pre-existing Ag over REBCO, wet-etch Ag in the future-CFD zones only; protect low-Ri stripes with resist mask. Rinse thoroughly; verify complete Ag removal in exposed zones by eddy-current thickness gauge and optical inspection.
- Step5.2 (Masking for CFD pattern): Apply photoresist via R2R coat, UV expose to open central 80% width (or DoE widths) while protecting 10% edge zones per side. Ensure mask alignment tolerance ±50 µm to maintain continuous edge stripes.
- Step5.3 (Amorphous barrier deposition): Deposit Al2O3 by R2R ALD at ≤120 °C to avoid oxygen loss from REBCO; thickness per DoE (2–5 nm). Alternative: RF sputter amorphous AlOx at room temperature with low power and high Ar/O₂ pressure to ensure amorphous film; minimize energetic bombardment. For barrier-free edge stripes, either (a) keep resist on edges during deposition or (b) post-deposition selectively wet-etch Al2O3 from edge zones (e.g., dilute NaOH or phosphoric acid, validated to avoid REBCO attack).
- Step5.4 (Resist strip and clean): Remove resist with solvent sequence (e.g., NMP/IPA), DI water rinse, N₂ dry. Confirm barrier absent in edge zones and present in CFD region by FTIR ellipsometry on witness foils processed in parallel and by XPS spot checks.
- Step5.5 (Ag stabilizer deposition): Deposit 2.5 µm Ag over the full width by DC magnetron sputtering at room temperature with low ion energy; use thickness monitors to ±5% control. This Ag layer makes direct contact with low-Ri edge stripes and sits atop the barrier in CFD zones, thus defining the patterned interfacial resistance.
- Step5.6 (Optional Cu overlayer): For mechanical robustness and terminal wetting, add 5 µm Cu by sputter or electroplate; keep total added thickness consistent across variants to maintain comparable thermal stabilization.
- Step5.7 (Reel-to-reel inspection): Inline eddy-current map of Ag/Cu thickness; optical line-scan to confirm pattern continuity; electrical continuity test along length.

Step6: Interface and microstructural verification:
- Cut short coupons (10–20 mm) from each variant for microprobe tests.
- TLM/CTLM fabrication: pattern Ag pads (50–200 µm spacing arrays) on top of barrier and on low-Ri zones to extract specific contact resistivity at 300 K and 77 K; fit to extract ρc and sheet resistance; select variants within 100–320 µΩ·cm² window.
- Cross-sectional TEM on at least one coupon per variant to verify amorphous layer continuity and thickness; EELS/EDX to confirm no significant interdiffusion into REBCO; ensure REBCO lattice remains ordered beneath (no amorphized REBCO layer).
- XRD on processed tapes: verify orthorhombic REBCO peaks unchanged, Δω and Δφ retained; absence of secondary phases indicative of REBCO degradation.
- AFM/SEM: assess surface roughness; check for pinholes or cracks in barrier zones after Ag deposition.

Step7: Electrical performance of processed tapes at 77 K:
- Measure Ic and n-value (1 µV cm⁻¹ criterion) for each processed tape (≥3 positions per 1 m length). Compare to baseline; accept if Ic degradation ≤5% and n≥20.
- Measure longitudinal E–I with careful subtraction of current-transfer voltage offset attributable to CFD zones (baseline E–I from control tapes used to de-embed).
- Verify DC stabilization: low-Ri edge stripes must provide low-resistance path at low fields; check uniformity of E–I across length.

Step8: Mechanical strain/bending tolerance tests:
- Mandrel tests: Bend processed tapes on mandrels corresponding to bending diameter ≥6.9 mm (per target), plus controls at tighter diameters, to map reversible and irreversible strain thresholds. Use strain formula for REBCO on metal substrate to keep axial compressive strain ≥−1% (absolute). Measure Ic before/after bending; target Ic retention ≥75% at 6.9 mm total bending diameter for CFD tapes.
- Cyclic bending (e.g., 100 cycles at target diameter) to ensure no delamination or barrier cracking; check Ic/n-value post cycling.

Step9: Thermal cycling and terminal preparation:
- Electro-deposit ~10 µm Cu pads on tape ends (length ~10–20 mm) to act as solder lands; verify thickness and adhesion by cross-section and pull test.
- Solderability test: Indium solder wetting at ≤160 °C under N₂; verify no significant Ag consumption and that REBCO is not thermally affected.
- Thermal cycling: 3–5 cycles between 300 K and 77 K; measure contact resistance (<1 µΩ·cm²) and Ic after cycles.

Step10: NZPV measurement on single tapes:
- Mount 20–30 cm sections on G10 holder with minimal thermal mass; attach 8–12 equally spaced voltage taps (e.g., 5–10 mm spacing) using pogo pins or spot-welded leads; four-probe current leads at ends.
- Immerse in pumped-LN₂ bath; stabilize temperature at 67, 72, and 77 K for parametric study; map temperature along sample with PT100 array (±0.05 K).
- Quench initiation: position NdFeB magnet at center; ramp current to desired value (e.g., 200–1000 A depending on Ic) and trigger quench by magnet application/removal; repeat with micro-heater pulses for reproducibility.
- Data acquisition: sample all taps at ≥100 kS/s; define voltage threshold (e.g., 0.1 V) and time-of-arrival method to compute NZPV; correct for inductive and baseline voltages using pre-quench reference; compute average and directional NZPV.
- Repeat for control (non-CFD) tapes under identical conditions. Fit NZPV vs current to power law; quantify enhancement factor for each variant.

Step11: CORC cable design and fabrication:
- Select copper former OD 6.35 mm; confirm total bending diameter ~6.9 mm at winding radius to limit compressive strain below −1%.
- Choose cable architecture: e.g., 2 layers with N tapes per layer (e.g., 6 tapes per layer, 12 total), 4 mm width, helical angles per standard CORC design to balance mechanical strain and current sharing; no interlayer insulation to allow current sharing.
- Use CFD tapes for all layers in one cable; fabricate a second identical cable with non-CFD tapes as control.
- Winding: Maintain constant tension; monitor angles; avoid kinks; ensure CFD low-Ri edges are not damaged; document tape positions.
- Terminations: Solder ends to copper end-caps using indium solder onto pre-plated Cu pads; use compressive fixtures to ensure uniform wetting; measure end-to-end DC resistance at 300 K to verify joint quality.

Step12: Cable-level electrical and mechanical qualification:
- Ic measurement at 77 K, self-field using pulsed-current; extract n-value; compare to sum of tape Ic expectations minus geometric/strain factors; confirm CFD cable retains ≥68–75% Ic after winding per target band.
- Axial strain tests: apply modest tensile/compressive loads to evaluate Ic sensitivity; ensure no excessive degradation.

Step13: Cable NZPV experiments:
- Instrument a 16–20 cm uniform section with a PCB-based pogo-pin voltage-tap array at ~5–6 mm spacing around the circumference to capture helical propagation; reference potential at ends; monitor multiple azimuthal positions to resolve front homogeneity.
- Thermal environment: pumped-LN₂ bath at 67–77 K; verify uniformity ±0.05 K along length via PT100s affixed to jacket.
- Quench initiation: place NdFeB magnet near the outer layer at mid-length; repeat with inner-layer excitation if accessible; optionally use a small resistive heater element epoxied to outer jacket to cross-check.
- Drive currents: 0.3–1.2 kA (bounded by cable Ic); for each current and temperature, record multi-channel voltage transients at ≥100 kS/s.
- Analysis: compute NZPV along cable by time-of-flight across taps; compare CFD vs control. Evaluate isotropy of propagation along helical path and across layers; quantify enhancement factor and dependence on current and temperature.

Step14: Modeling and interpretation:
- Use a 2D/3D electro-thermal model of tape/cable cross-section (finite-element or equivalent circuit) to extract effective current transfer length from measured NZPV and interface resistivity; include contact resistivity values from TLM and thermal properties of Ag/Cu/Hastelloy.
- Compare model predictions to measured NZPV scaling; identify optimal interfacial resistance and coverage that maximize NZPV without causing excessive steady-state losses.

Step15: Quench detection/protection benchmarking:
- Implement a voltage-based detector with programmable thresholds (e.g., 50–200 mV) and time delays (1–5 ms). Using the measured NZPV and cable inductance, determine minimum detectable voltage and time-to-detection at operating currents.
- Demonstrate repeated quench-and-dump cycles without hotspot damage: trigger quench at set current, detect within target milliseconds, open circuit or divert current; post-test inspect tapes/cable for damage via optical microscopy and continuity checks.

Step16: Reliability and endurance:
- Perform 20–50 quench cycles on a CFD cable at 77 K and 0.7–0.9 Ic; periodically remeasure Ic and n-value; inspect for delamination or barrier degradation.
- Thermal cycling of full cable (5–10 cycles between 300 K and 77 K) with Ic and joint resistance measurements after each cycle.

Step17: Risk mitigation and process optimization:
- If Ic degradation >5% after CFD processing: reduce barrier deposition temperature, switch to lower-energy deposition (ALD preferred), verify chemical compatibility of etchants, and widen low-Ri edge stripes slightly to reduce added series resistance.
- If interfacial resistance is outside 100–320 µΩ·cm²: adjust barrier thickness in 0.5–1 nm increments; validate by TLM at both 300 K and 77 K before large-scale runs.
- If NZPV enhancement <4×: increase CFD coverage incrementally (e.g., from 80% to 90%) or slightly raise interfacial resistance within acceptable range; verify that Ic and n-value remain within targets.
- If joints show resistance drift: increase Cu pad thickness or switch to Au flash over Cu before soldering; verify solder profile.

Step18: Documentation and reporting:
- Record full process parameters (mask dimensions, deposition rates, temperatures), metrology results (XRD, TLM, TEM), electrical data (Ic, n-value), mechanical tests, thermal cycling, NZPV datasets, and model parameters.
- Summarize best-performing CFD design (coverage and ρc) with uncertainty analysis; compile comparison of CFD vs control at tape and cable levels, including detection thresholds and protection timings.

Step19: Scale-up validation:
- Run 10–50 m R2R tape with the selected CFD recipe; perform in-line QC and sample every 5 m for Ic/n/TLM; assemble at least one additional CORC cable from this lot to confirm reproducibility.

Step20: Safety and compliance:
- Enforce cryogenic and high-current safety protocols (interlocks, insulated bus bars, quench dump resistors).
- Dispose of chemical wastes per regulations; ensure proper ventilation for ALD/sputtering effluents.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1 – Single-tape pre-characterisation  
- Measure Ic and n-value at 77 K, self-field, on the individual CFD and regular REBCO tapes intended for cabling (1 µV cm⁻¹ criterion).  

Step 2 – Bending-strain screening  
- Wind sample tapes (REBCO side facing former) on copper formers of decreasing diameter; record retained Ic after 45° bend.  
- Select the smallest former diameter that keeps Ic degradation ≤32 %; adopt 6.35 mm-OD copper rod + two heat-shrink layers → 6.9 mm bending diameter for cable winding.  

Step 3 – CFD tape preparation (reel-to-reel)  
- Mask 0.8 mm-wide stripes along both edges of 1 m-long SP REBCO tapes.  
- Chemically etch unmasked silver (aqueous H₂O₂:NH₄OH:H₂O 1:1:4) to create a high-resistivity degraded layer (Ri 100–320 µΩ cm²) under the future silver over-coat; remove mask; deposit silver.  
- Electroplate 10 µm Cu on 9–10 cm end sections (C1 & C3) to enable low-temperature indium soldering without Ag consumption.  
- Leave 50 cm sacrificial tail (C4) for winding grip; final usable length 30 cm.  

Step 4 – Regular tape preparation  
- Same length (1 m) and Cu-plated ends (D1 & D3) but no CFD patterning.  

Step 5 – CORC® cable winding  
- Wind two contra-helical layers (3 tapes each, 38.6° inner, 37.7° outer twist angle, 17 mm twist pitch) on the insulated 6.9 mm former; no inter-layer material added.  
- Cut sacrificial tails; obtain 30 cm active cable length.  
- Insert each cable end into a Cu tube (ID 9.4 mm, OD 12.7 mm); fill with indium solder to form 3 cm (regular) or 4 cm (CFD) termination.  

Step 6 – Room-temperature resistance check  
- Four-terminal measurement through termination voltage taps: 52 mΩ (CFD) and 44 mΩ (regular).  

Step 7 – Critical-current measurement  
- Immerse cable in liquid-N₂ (77 K) or in pumped-cryostat (65–77 K, ±0.05 K homogeneity).  
- Inject square current pulses (pulse width ≤ few 10 ms for NZPV, DC ramp for Ic).  
- Record total cable voltage; subtract terminal current-transfer component (baseline fit); apply 1 µV cm⁻¹ criterion to extract Ic and n-value.  
- Repeat for 67–77 K range on CFD cable; single-point calibration (76 K → 77 K, factor 1.15) used for regular cable.  

Step 8 – Normal-zone propagation velocity (NZPV) measurement  
- Mount 16 cm PCB equipped with spring-loaded pogo pins every 5.9 mm (one pin per outer-layer tape per twist pitch).  
- Place small NdFeB magnets under cable to create an 8 mm-long local Ic-depressed zone; trigger quench with a single current pulse.  
- Acquire pin voltages at ≥kHz sampling via multi-channel DAQ; define arrival time when local voltage reaches 0.1 V.  
- Compute NZPV = tap separation / time difference between successive taps; average left- and right-going fronts.  
- Sweep current 300–1200 A at 77 K; repeat in cryostat at 68.6, 71.3, 73.5, 77.3 K.  

Step 9 – Post-mortem inspection  
- Visually check for burn marks or degradation (regular cable failed at magnet location after 73.5 K run).  

[Experimental Design Details]
- Samples: 4 mm-wide SP REBCO tapes, 50 µm Hastelloy, 1.6 µm REBCO, 2.5 µm total Ag, no additional Cu stabiliser on cable section.  
- CFD zone: 3.2 mm width (f = 0.8), 26 cm length along each tape, Ri 100–320 µΩ cm².  
- Cable: 6 tapes, 2 layers, opposite twist, 30 cm active length, 6.9 mm final winding diameter.  
- Temperature: 65–77 K controlled by pumping on LN₂ bath; PT100 sensors at 4, 8, 12 cm heights.  
- Current: pulsed square wave (NZPV) or DC ramp (Ic); max ≈1.2 kA.  
- Electric-field criterion: 1 µV cm⁻¹ for Ic; 0.1 V for NZPV arrival time.  
- Voltage contacts: total cable taps for Ic; 5.9 mm-spaced pogo pins for NZPV.  
- Magnetic trigger: NdFeB cylinders, 8 mm influence length, placed inside sample-holder holes.
